articles.title: Scientists create a brain-to-brain network that lets people communicate without words, offering a breakthrough for human communication
articles.summary: Science News: Scientists have demonstrated direct brain-to-brain communication using a system that transmitted information between people without speech, typing or .
articles.body: Scientists have demonstrated direct brain-to-brain communication using a system that transmitted information between people without speech, typing or physical gestures. The research led to ‘BrainNet,’ a system that connected three people and allowed them to collaborate on a task using brain signals. Electrical activity was recorded from the brain and transmitted over the internet, while magnetic stimulation delivered the information to another participant’s brain. The experiment did not enable participants to read complete thoughts or communicate freely, but it showed that information linked to a person’s decision could be extracted from brain activity and transmitted to another brain. The findings provide an early demonstration of a multi-person brain-to-brain communication network.How did scientists begin connecting human brainsThe story behind BrainNet began before the three-person experiment. According to the MIT Technology Review researchers had already demonstrated in 2015 that two people could be connected through a brain-to-brain interface. That earlier experiment involved a game similar to 20 Questions. One person could use brain activity to communicate information to another person, showing that brain signals could carry enough information for a simple question-and-answer interaction.The next challenge was that if two brains could exchange information, could several brains be connected into the same system? The BrainNet researchers set out to answer that question. Their findings, described in the paper ‘BrainNet: A Multi-Person Brain-to-Brain Interface for Direct Collaboration Between Brains,’ presented what they described as the first multi-person, non-invasive direct brain-to-brain interface designed for collaborative problem-solving.BrainNet allowing people to communicate without speakingBrainNet combined two technologies named electroencephalography (EEG) and transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The MIT review explained that EEG equipment uses electrodes placed on the head to detect electrical activity produced by the brain. The system can recognise particular patterns associated with a person's decision. TMS, meanwhile, was used to send information into another person's brain. Rather than requiring an implant, the technique uses magnetic stimulation applied from outside the head.The research paper explains that two participants acted as ‘senders,’ while a third participant became the ‘receiver.’ The senders watched a Tetris-like game and decided whether a falling block should be rotated before it was dropped. Their decisions were detected through EEG and transmitted through the internet. The receiver could not see the game screen. Instead, information from the two senders was delivered to the receiver's brain through magnetic stimulation of the visual area at the back of the brain. The receiver then used brain activity to make the final decision.Was this experiment really a hive mindNot quite. The phrase ‘hive mind’ makes the achievement sound more advanced than it was. BrainNet did not allow participants to read complete thoughts, hear sentences inside each other's heads or freely communicate whatever they wanted. The system was designed to transmit very limited pieces of information connected to a specific task. That limitation is important. The researchers were not creating a shared consciousness. They were demonstrating that a carefully designed system could take a small amount of information from one brain, send it electronically and use stimulation to deliver that information to another brain.Still, the experiment introduced something genuinely new. The receiver was not simply getting one person's decision. Two senders could provide information, allowing the receiver to combine their signals before deciding what to do. The system also included another round in which the senders could provide feedback on the receiver's decision. The research paper noted that five groups of three participants successfully used BrainNet, achieving an average accuracy of about 81.3% on the task.Could the receiver tell which brain was more reliableOne of the most interesting parts of the experiment was not simply whether the system worked, but ‘how the receiver handled information from different people.’ The researchers deliberately made one sender's information less reliable by adding ‘noise’ to that person's signal. The receiver was then able to learn which sender was providing more dependable information. According to the study, receivers could distinguish between the reliability of the senders using the information delivered through BrainNet and favour the more reliable source when making decisions. That feature is what made the researchers compare the system with a social network. In ordinary human groups, people naturally learn whose information can be trusted. BrainNet showed a basic version of that process taking place through direct brain-to-brain communication.What could a network of connected brains eventually becomeThe researchers were careful about what the experiment actually demonstrated, but its possible implications were much broader. The MIT Technology Review described BrainNet as a ‘world-first brain-to-brain network’ and highlighted its potential as a new form of communication. The researchers themselves suggested that future systems could involve larger numbers of people. The research paper noted that the current system used two senders and one receiver, but that the concept could potentially be expanded to include more participants. With suitable equipment, each person could also potentially send and receive information through the brain interface.That possibility raises the prospect of people collaborating on tasks while bypassing some conventional forms of communication. For now, BrainNet remains a carefully controlled research demonstration rather than a real-world telepathic network. It showed that human brains could become nodes in a network where information moves from one brain, through technology, and into another. The idea of a ‘social network of brains’ may still sound like science fiction. BrainNet showed that its first basic building blocks are already possible.

articles.title: Nature invented biodegradable plastic millions of years ago and animals have been eating it ever since; scientists now think it could offer a clue to Earth’s plastic crisis
articles.summary: Science News: Long before humans learned how to turn petroleum into bottles and bags and packaging, nature had already invented her own plastic. These natural polym.
articles.body: Long before humans learned how to turn petroleum into bottles and bags and packaging, nature had already invented her own plastic. These natural polymers have been made for hundreds of millions of years hidden inside microorganisms living in soils, sediments and oceans – and new research suggests animals have been eating and breaking them down for almost as long. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Marine Microbiology in Bremen, Germany, found that a surprisingly wide range of animals have enzymes that can break down polyhydroxyalkanoates, or PHAs. These natural substances are produced by microorganisms as a carbon and energy reservoir, and are now being developed as biodegradable alternatives to conventional plastics. A report published by Science Daily states that the finding may provide new insights into how carbon is cycled through ecosystems and may also help scientists understand the potential for biodegradable plastics in a world struggling with plastic pollution.Nature’s first plasticMany bacteria and archaea naturally produce PHAs. If microorganisms have excess carbon they do not need, they can convert it into PHA and store it within their cells. For the uninitiated, PHAs are very similar to an energy reserve in that way. PHAs can be degraded by biological processes, unlike traditional plastics that may persist in the environment for long periods. They occur naturally in soils, sediments and aquatic environments, making them one of the relatively few naturally produced plastic-like materials that are fully biodegradable. Scientists have known that microorganisms can degrade these compounds. Less certain was whether animals could access the carbon stored within microbial PHAs. Now, a study published in the journal Nature Ecology & Evolution has shown that they can.A strange marine worm gives the clueIf we go by the report, the study began with an unusual marine worm, Olavius algarvensis. The little animal has neither a mouth nor a digestive tract. Instead, it relies on the bacteria that live under its skin. The worm derives its nutrients from digesting its bacterial partners, establishing a unique relationship between animal and microorganism. Researchers found that one of the worm’s bacterial symbionts stores a lot of carbon in the form of PHA. That raised an interesting question: had the worm evolved a way to break down that material and tap its stored carbon? Scientists found an enzyme in a worm that can break down PHAs into smaller molecules that animals can utilize. High-resolution imaging suggests the enzyme is produced by the worm in the same place where it digests its bacterial partners. The finding implies that the worm is able to tap the energy stores of its symbiotic bacteria.The ability is not limited to one wormAlso, the finding became even more significant when researchers looked beyond Olavius algarvensis. Looking at animal genomes, the team found related enzymes in more than 66 species in nine different animal groups. Further evidence came from laboratory experiments. Enzymes from distantly related animals, including a sponge, an earthworm and a springtail, also degraded PHAs. The researchers were surprised at that wide distribution, as the studied species are separated by huge evolutionary distances. This points out that the ability to consume these naturally occurring microbial plastics may be far more widespread among animals than scientists previously thought.From microbial reserve to bioplasticThis is especially interesting because humans have started making PHAs for many of the same properties that make them useful in nature. It is reported that industrial PHA is produced by growing bacteria in fermentation tanks and feeding them with carbon-rich materials such as sugars, starches or plant oils. The microorganisms accumulate large amounts of PHA under appropriate conditions. It can then be harvested and turned into products that are like plastic. Also, materials based on PHA are moldable and stable enough to be used for various applications. They are being developed and used in applications such as food packaging, hygiene products and agriculture.In agriculture, PHA beads can encapsulate fertilizers and release them slowly as the material breaks down. Medical uses include wound dressings, pharmaceutical delivery systems, resorbable implants and sutures designed to degrade in vivo. They are appealing in part because of their biological circularity: they can be produced by microorganisms, but they can also be broken down by biological processes.Can animals help to close the biological loop?The new findings give a new twist to that cycle. The report states that if animals are naturally endowed with enzymes able to degrade PHAs, they could take part, together with the microorganisms, in the degradation of these compounds in ecosystems. That could make it easier for microbial carbon, thought to be locked away inside bacterial cells, to enter animal food webs. How common and significant this process is in nature is still being worked out by scientists. They do not yet know how much carbon moves through this pathway globally, or how significant animal digestion of PHA is relative to microbial degradation. But the finding alters the way scientists think about the relationship between microorganisms and the animals that consume them.What the plastic crisis is all aboutThese findings, however, should not be considered evidence that animals can simply solve the world’s plastic pollution problem. PHAs are inherently different to the conventional plastics which dominate current waste streams. Most of the plastic accumulating in landfills, oceans and ecosystems is not made from microbial PHAs and is not necessarily capable of being broken down using the enzymes found in this research. Instead, the research points to a biological system that has been around for a very long time. It is important to note that this knowledge could eventually help scientists design better biodegradable materials or understand how new bioplastics behave when they enter natural environments.Images Courtesy: istock

articles.title: CERN, where scientists smash particles at nearly the speed of light, has a 2-metre Shiva Nataraja statue outside; why India gifted the cosmic dancer to the physics lab in 2004
articles.summary: Science News: For those who don’t know, CERN is Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire (European Council for Nuclear Research). It is the world's largest part.
articles.body: For those who don’t know, CERN is Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire (European Council for Nuclear Research). It is the world's largest particle physics laboratory near Geneva, Switzerland (near Franco-Swiss border). It is the lab where scientists accelerate particles to almost the speed of light. But beyond this fact, what surprises people when they enter this space is the unusual statue standing right in the centre of the campuses of one of the world's most advanced centres of particle physics. It is a 2-metre-tall bronze figure of Shiva in his Nataraja form, the cosmic dancer.Let’s find out more about the cosmic statue:A gift from IndiaThe statue was a gift from India. It was gifted in 2004, and its presence is more than a cultural tribute. It represents a striking metaphor of the ancient Indian image of cosmic creation and destruction with the modern scientific attempt to understand the universe at its smallest scales.The statue, for Indian travellers, offers an intriguing reminder that the search for answers about the universe is not confined to lab or equations. Sometimes, it is also about thousands of years of mythology and art.What does the lab do?The laboratory is trying to recreate conditions of the early universe. It is officially the world's largest particle physics laboratory equipped with the most famous machine, the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). Not many must be aware of the fact that it is the world's largest and most powerful particle accelerator.Understanding the LHCSo, LHC is a 27-kilometre ring lying about 100 metres underground. Inside it, two beams of particles travel in opposite directions at close to the speed of light before being brought into collision. Scientists study what emerges from these collisions to investigate the fundamental particles and forces that make up our universe.One of the extraordinary things CERN can do is recreate some of the extreme conditions believed to have existed in the universe's earliest moments.And standing above this extraordinary underground world of collisions is Shiva.Why did India give CERN a statue of Nataraja?The answer goes back to India's long scientific relationship with CERN.India's collaboration with the laboratory dates to the 1960s, and Indian scientists and institutions have played an important role in CERN's programmes. In June 2004, India gifted CERN a 2-metre-tall statue of Shiva Nataraja to celebrate this longstanding scientific partnership.The statue was unveiled on June 18, 2004, by CERN Director-General Robert Aymar, Indian Atomic Energy Commission chairman Anil Kakodkar and India's ambassador K. M. Chandrasekhar.Tandav meets quantum physicsThe answer is because Shiva's cosmic dance offered a powerful metaphor for the dynamic universe being investigated by particle physicists.The Nataraja is not simply Shiva depicted dancing. The image represents a universe in perpetual movement—creation, transformation and destruction.That symbolism fascinated physicist and author Fritjof Capra, who explored the relationship between the imagery of Shiva's cosmic dance and modern physics. Capra first discussed the parallel in a 1972 article and later made it a central metaphor in his 1975 book The Tao of Physics.Classical physics encouraged an image of matter as consisting of solid, stable building blocks. Quantum physics revealed a far stranger microscopic world in which particles interact, transform and emerge in processes governed by quantum fields.As the plaque beside CERN's statue explains through Capra's words, “For the modern physicists, then, Shiva's dance is the dance of subatomic matter.”The plaque goes on to connect the ancient bronze images of dancing Shiva with the patterns revealed through modern physics, describing the metaphor as a meeting point between ancient mythology, religious art and modern science.A statue worth seeking out on a CERN visitThe Nataraja statue adds an unexpected cultural dimension to a visit to CERN.The laboratory's public spaces and exhibitions introduce visitors to particle physics, while the statue outside offers a very different way of contemplating the same enormous question: what is the universe made of, and how does it work?There is no claim that the statue represents a scientific theory, nor that Hindu philosophy and quantum mechanics are scientifically equivalent. Instead, its significance lies in the metaphor—a centuries-old artistic representation of cosmic motion standing beside a modern laboratory devoted to uncovering the behaviour of matter at its most fundamental level.

articles.title: In 2022, scientists covered soil with 5 to 10 millimetres of wax-coated sand, slowing evaporation and increasing crop yields by up to 73%
articles.summary: Science News: Discover how scientists from KAUST innovated with wax-coated sand to combat evaporation, increase soil moisture, and enhance crop yields by up to 73% in arid regions like Saudi Arabia.
articles.body: In arid regions, farmers face the challenge of producing food while working with limited freshwater supplies. In Saudi Arabia, where agriculture relies heavily on irrigation, reducing water loss from cultivated soil is an important challenge. Plastic mulch film has long been used to reduce soil moisture loss by covering the soil surface. Although effective, conventional plastic mulch can generate substantial waste when it is removed after the growing season. In a 2022 study published in ACS Agricultural Science & Technology, a group of scientists from King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) developed a simple alternative: instead of plastic, they used water-repellent sand.Turning ordinary sand into a water barrierThe research was led by Himanshu Mishra, a KAUST bioengineer whose lab has studied superhydrophobic materials for years. These are surfaces so water-repellent that water beads slide off them. Nature can do this too: desert beetles, plants, and animals have water-repellent coatings that help them capture moisture.Mishra's team asked whether that same trick could be applied at agricultural scale, using one of the most abundant materials on Earth: ordinary sand. The researchers dissolved purified paraffin wax in hexane and coated ordinary silica sand with the solution. As the solvent evaporated, it left a thin layer of paraffin wax, about 20 nanometers thick, on each grain, making the sand highly water-repellent.In a KAUST press release titled Wax coating helps waning water resources,Mishra said the mulch layer, when added to wet soil, "greatly reduces evaporation." Exposed agricultural soil can lose substantial amounts of water through evaporation, particularly under hot, dry and windy conditions. The superhydrophobic layer creates a barrier at the soil surface that slows the movement of water into the air.The results: Lower evaporation and higher yieldsAccording to the peer-reviewed results, 5- to 10-millimeter-thick mulch layers reduced evaporation from soil by 56% to 78% and increased soil moisture content by 25% to 45%. Under freshwater irrigation, yields of tomato, barley, and wheat increased by 17% to 73%. Under harsher conditions, when tomato and barley were irrigated with brackish water containing 5,500 ppm salt, yields increased by 53% to 208% compared with non-mulched plots.A separate 2022 study published in Plant-Environment Interactions found that tomato plants grown with the mulch developed a significantly larger root xylem system, a tissue involved in transporting water and nutrients through the plant. The mulched plants also produced about 30% more fruit than unmulched plants.Why wax-coated sand instead of plasticOne potential advantage of the approach is that the researchers use sand as the main mulch material rather than conventional plastic film. The sand is coated with a thin layer of paraffin wax during preparation, and the resulting material can be applied directly to the soil surface. The researchers also examined soil bacterial communities near plant roots and reported no significant changes in their composition in the tested conditions. The environmental and economic implications of producing and applying the coated sand at large agricultural scales, however, still require further evaluation.What’s nextAfter those early tests, the KAUST team tried SandX on other crops and local trees in Saudi Arabia and began working toward larger-scale production after receiving an innovation grant from the university. The researchers are now investigating whether the treated sand can deliver similar water-saving and productivity benefits across a wider range of crops and growing conditions.

articles.title: Babies made from stem cells. Same sex couples with no donors. This is the future of fertility
articles.summary: Advancements in fertility are going places you'd never imagine. Legal and ethical scholars are trying to keep up.
articles.body:
The first successful human pregnancy using in vitro fertilization, or IVF , was nearly 50 years ago.

Today, there are more than 100,000 babies born annually through IVF in the United States, according to the Society for Assisted Reproductive Technology .

And 20 years from now, Harvard University professor Ivan Glenn Cohen believes it will be possible to create human life from stem cells − starting with skin cells, with no need for invasive egg retrievals. Stem cell fertility treatments could come to clinics even sooner, within a decade, according to Henry Greely , a Stanford professor who specializes in the ethical, legal and social implications of new biomedical technologies and whose provocatively-titled book "The End of Sex" published in 2016.

It's called in vitro gametogenesis, or IVG, and it's one of several developing fertility technologies being tested around the world. Cohen , a leading expert on the intersection of bioethics and law, told USA TODAY this technology could eventually make it possible for same-sex couples to reproduce without a donor, for more than two people to have a genetic connection to one child or for a single person to procreate on their own. Proponents say these advances will change medicine and are the long-awaited next frontier in fertility. Critics argue some implications may be unethical.

"It is one of the things that people have dreamt about for many years," says Dr. Thomas Molinaro, a board-certified reproductive endocrinologist, obstetrician and gynecologist, and chief medical officer of Everleap Fertility. He adds that several groups are working on this research now, "but I think we're still a long way off from this being routine and something that is offered as a treatment."

Other inventions that might sound like science fiction to some are being developed across the globe to help with human conception and gestation, including genome editing and artificial wombs. The future of fertility is full of possibilities, including a world in which humans could have the option to create an embryo in a petri dish from skin cells, edit the embryo's genetic composition and grow that child to term in a machine without compromising the physical health of the baby's parents. This hypothetical opens up a lot of fear, for some, about eugenics and the possibility of creating workforces or defense forces with traits tailored to efficiency. It sounds far-fetched, but science moves relatively quickly, Greely says. A lot could happen in the next 50 years.

But just because science has this potential, should humans pursue a world in which babies can be made in machines? What would that world look like? Would it solve declining birth rates and fertility struggles , or create new problems? While scientists move forward and commercial investors buy in, legal and ethical scholars are trying to keep pace.

"I don't think there's such a thing as thinking about something too early when it comes to the future of reproduction, because this kind of stuff will fundamentally change the way that we (make babies)," says Elizabeth Chloe Romanis, a biolaw professor at Durham Law School. "Everybody has a really strong stake in it."

Romanis' research is focused on ectogenesis, or the possibility of machines that could "just grow babies from scratch for us." Full ectogenesis is probably 50 years from humans, she says, but scientists at the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia have successfully taken a premature fetal lamb from its mother's womb, placed it in a womb-like machine and carried the fetus to term there . The goal, researchers say, is to provide better outcomes for premature human babies. But full ectogenesis could be good for women with diabetes or other pregnancy-related illnesses, or someone diagnosed with cancer during pregnancy. It could eventually become an alternative to surrogacy .

"Some people argue ectogestation is a solution to women's inequality," Romanis says, but she's not so sure. Society treats pregnant people poorly, she says, labeling them as economically unproductive and potentially risky toward their fetus. That could get worse with ectogenesis, she says, if ectogestation is seen as safer than women's bodies.

"There is a deep and I think passionate split in the feminist movement about ectogenesis, where one wing says, 'This is patriarchy's final attempt to get rid of us altogether. If they don't need our wombs, then they don't need us,'" Greely says. "And the other wing says, 'This is so liberating, we can have children without having to be pregnant.'"

If we've learned anything from IVF, it's that it's a business, says Nava Dimer, director of reproductive bioethics for Rader Law Group and IVF Law Group − "the business of creating families."

Yet the pace of advancement in fertility technology doesn't always leave room for stakeholders to stop and think about the broader impact it might have on people, says Sonia Suter, professor of law and founding director of the Health Law and Policy Program at The George Washington University.

"What worries me the most," she says, "is a lot of the biggest efforts are happening in the commercial sector." She adds, "The capacity and the wisdom of developing these technologies are two very different things."

The target audience for any fertility technology is someone who wants to be a parent. That desire, Dimer says, can put people in a vulnerable position.

"If standing on your head resulted in more successful pregnancies, many of my patients would stand on their head for eight hours a day," Molinaro says.

IVG has been successful in animal birth trials, Cohen and Greely say, and human embryos have been created this way. "Nobody has done it (for) human reproduction all the way," Cohen says, adding that the United States prohibits IVG births in humans and any research on embryos older than 14 days. Biomedical companies in the United States are campaigning to loosen embryonic research restrictions, and in the meantime other countries in Europe and Asia are forging on in hopes to bring IVG to patients as soon as possible.

While it's exciting that scientists have successfully taken IVG to live births in mice, Greely says, "mice aren't people. And even if you can do it, the safety issues are huge."

Dr. Paula Amato, director of the Oregon Health & Science University's Division of Reproductive Endocrinology & Infertility, is one of the researchers working on IVG. The human embryos her team has made, she says, lacked certain chromosomes after fertilization.

Still, she thinks the technology could be ready for human clinical trials in about 10 to 15 years, giving same-sex couples, menopausal women, cancer survivors and others who currently can't reproduce a chance.

While giving same-sex couples the opportunity to have genetically-related children could be an argument for equality, Cohen and others worry about society's obsession with genetic connectedness. The LGBTQ+ community has spent a lot of time emphasizing that genetic connection doesn't matter so much, Suter says. Would IVG undermine the value of chosen family?

"The ethical questions here, I think, are wrapped up in some cultural wars that we're experiencing in this country," Suter says. The resistance some people have to same-sex parents "let alone genetic parents," she says, could lead to potential backlash.

IVG could also give people the option to reproduce with multiple partners by "collapsing generations," Suter says. Cells from two people could create one embryo, and cells from another two people could create another embryo, and then scientists could create egg and sperm from those embryos to create another embryo, in several iterations. In theory, Greely says, 16 people could have a child together with IVG. "They'd be like great-great grandchildren," Suter says.

And then there's the wildest possibility, Greely says, of a single genetic parent to what he calls a "unibaby." It's different from cloning, Suter says, because the person's offspring through IVG "wouldn't be the exact identical mix of genes." Who would want to do this? Solo parents, Suter says, who want to avoid the personal or legal challenges that can arise from using donor gametes.

"But it does raise some ethical concerns about safety," Suter says, "because it's a bit like having incest on steroids."

Anna Louie Sussman, a journalist and cultural critic who wrote "Inconceivable" on her own fertility journey, says IVG "sounds nice," but she's not sure what it will look like in practice. Enduring a small skin biopsy that doesn't even need stitches is "obviously preferable to shooting yourself up with hormones," she says. But what will the monetary price be, and what about success rates?

"I would imagine most people prefer the old-fashioned way," Sussman says. "It's free."

Genome editing, 'designer babies' and the slippery slope to eugenics

One of the arguments in favor of expanding IVF and eventually IVG, Greely says, is the ability to screen for genetic diseases in embryos through a technology called preimplantation genetic testing, or PGT.

Several companies are working to make the IVF process better and more efficient with the help of robotics, automation and artificial intelligence. The hope is that it's cheaper and more accessible, giving more potential parents the option to prevent diseases like spina bifida, sickle cell disease and other disorders in their babies.

But it's a slippery slope, and some of this technology is "bordering on eugenics," Dimer says.

The tension between embryonic genetic testing and the disability community is palpable.

"I think part of it is just kind of deciding, as a country, what do we think are appropriate uses of reproductive technologies?" Suter says, adding that many countries have restricted testing for serious health conditions. "The U.S. is pretty laissez-faire about this."

Dr. David Sable, who has been at the forefront of IVF and founded companies including Assisted Reproductive Medical Technologies and Reprogenetics, says screening for some diseases like cystic fibrosis is easy, but the math is much harder for other diseases. It's even more difficult to screen for consumer traits like hair color, eye color, athletic ability, perfect pitch and intelligence. "It's not like ordering a salad from a takeout place," Sable says, disputing the possibility of "designer babies" outright.

Molinaro, too, says this technology is "largely considered experimental." That doesn't mean some companies aren't trying to capitalize on the possibility of genetically selecting, or someday even editing, embryos to have those traits.

"It's being offered to patients and marketed to patients," Sable says. "Depending on who you talk to, validation is a work in progress."

Little to no regulation means these companies "don't have to prove to anybody that they're accurate," Greely says. "And they're selling it for a nice profit."

And if not just embryo selection, but heritable human genome editing, is possible, Cohen says, what then? There are reports that a scientist in China already was successful in gene editing, which "many people view as problematic and unethical," Cohen says. That scientist, He Jiankui, was sentenced to three years in jail after after the twin girls at the center of these allegations were born, American Association for the Advancement of Science reported in 2019.

Embryo selection can have elements of eugenics and possibly sends "negative signals to disability communities," Cohen says. But with gene editing, "it's kind of on steroids because there's no limit to how much of this you can do."

There's an argument, Cohen says, that genetic selection of embryos isn't so different from the donor selection process. "We have these catalogs full of people, and they compare them," he says. "They're like, what were their LSAT scores? How beautiful? How tall is she? Where did she go to school?"

But really, Cohen says, most people's interests in growing their family don't hinge on heritable traits.

"Most people have actually very similar interests: I want a child that's healthy, I want a child that's going to live long, I want a child that's going to be happy," he says. "So it's not, like, so bespoke."

articles.title: Starship, da SpaceX, retorna da órbita e é capturada pelos braços mecânicos da plataforma de lançamento | G1

articles.summary: Representantes da SpaceX afirmaram que a captura deste sábado demonstra a capacidade de reutilização completa da Starship, projetada para viagens à Lua e a Marte.
articles.body:
A Starship, da SpaceX , retornou à Terra neste sábado (14), capturada no ar por braços mecânicos na mesma plataforma de lançamento de onde havia partido.

Starship, da SpaceX, retorna da órbita e é capturada pelos braços mecânicos da plataforma de lançamento — Foto: Reprodução/ Spacex

Foi o final esperado por Elon Musk e sua equipe: a primeira captura de uma Starship que retornava do espaço. Mas, com a explosão do propulsor de primeiro estágio pouco depois da decolagem na sexta-feira (13), no Texas , a empresa não conseguiu realizar a dupla captura que pretendia.

Destroços permaneceram no Golfo do México, isolados por boias, enquanto a espaçonave de aço inoxidável, em formato de projétil, descia na vertical até a plataforma de lançamento.

A captura espetacular, digna de um filme de ficção científica, ajudou a ofuscar o fracasso na recuperação do propulsor.

"Vocês conseguem acreditar?", exclamou Dan Huot, comentarista da SpaceX.

Representantes da SpaceX afirmaram que a captura deste sábado demonstra a capacidade de reutilização completa da Starship, projetada para viagens à Lua e a Marte. Embora a tentativa de recuperação do propulsor na sexta-feira tenha fracassado, a empresa já havia realizado outras três capturas bem-sucedidas, validando a técnica.

A Nasa comemorou a notícia deste sábado. A agência espacial está pagando bilhões de dólares pelo desenvolvimento da Starship para transportar astronautas da missão Artemis até a superfície da Lua ainda nesta década e ajudar na construção de uma base lunar permanente. As ambições de Musk são ainda maiores: ele quer lançar uma frota de Starships para construir uma cidade em Marte.

O maior e mais potente foguete do mundo — um colosso de 124 metros de altura — decolou no fim da tarde de sexta-feira da base da SpaceX para a Starship, perto da fronteira entre os Estados Unidos e o México. Após se separar sem problemas do propulsor, antes de os problemas começarem, a espaçonave do segundo estágio chegou à órbita e liberou 26 satélites avançados da rede Starlink.

A Starship continuou dando voltas ao redor da Terra a uma altitude de 265 quilômetros, transmitindo imagens ao vivo de si mesma e do planeta por meio da Starlink. A espaçonave completou 14 voltas ao redor da Terra, superando com folga o desempenho da missão anterior, que havia realizado entre uma e duas voltas.

Foi o 15º voo de uma Starship em escala real desde 2023 e apenas sua segunda viagem à órbita.

A SpaceX informou que todos os sistemas da espaçonave, incluindo o escudo térmico, essencial para a reentrada na atmosfera, aparentemente funcionaram bem.

Quanto ao propulsor, Kate Tice, da SpaceX, afirmou que seus motores pararam de funcionar antes do previsto durante a descida. O sistema de orientação do foguete detectou que ele não estava na posição correta e iniciou automaticamente o desvio para a água e a autodestruição. Os engenheiros ainda investigam as causas do problema.

A SpaceX espera começar a lançar Starships da Estação da Força Espacial de Cabo Canaveral, na Flórida, nos próximos meses. O local será o ponto de partida da próxima missão Artemis da Nasa, que não irá à Lua e permanecerá em órbita da Terra para realizar testes de acoplamento com o módulo de pouso lunar.

Os quatro astronautas da Artemis III tentarão acoplar sua cápsula não apenas à Starship, mas também à Blue Moon, da Blue Origin. As duas empresas se alternarão no transporte de tripulações até a superfície lunar. A Nasa tem como meta realizar a Artemis IV em 2028, o que representaria o primeiro pouso de seres humanos na Lua desde a era Apollo, há mais de meio século.

articles.title: A ‘yellow brick road’ was discovered 1,029 metres beneath the Pacific Ocean; scientists explain how volcanic rock and iron-rich deposits created the striking formation
articles.summary: A strange formation resembling a yellow brick road was discovered on the Pacific Ocean floor during an expedition by the Ocean Exploration Trust’s
articles.body: A strange formation resembling a yellow brick road was discovered on the Pacific Ocean floor during an expedition by the Ocean Exploration Trust’s research vessel E/V Nautilus. The structure was found at a depth of 1,029 metres near Nootka Seamount, within the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. Its unusually regular pattern made it resemble a brick sidewalk, but scientists identified it as a natural geological formation.According to a report published by The Oceanography Society on the Ocean Exploration Trust’s 2022 field season, the formation likely consists of fractured hyaloclastite, a type of volcanic rock created when hot magma meets cold water. Researchers suggested that its yellow colour likely resulted from low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of the volcanic glass.Scientists spotted a yellow brick road 1,029 metres beneath the PacificThe unusual pattern was observed during an E/V Nautilus expedition in the Pacific. The formation lay at a depth of 1,029 metres near Nootka Seamount, inside Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument. Its fractures intersect at right angles, giving it the look of a brick sidewalk. The resemblance prompted the description ‘yellow brick road’, but the appearance did not indicate that people had built or laid anything there.The report identifies the feature as a geological formation on the seafloor. It was one of several discoveries documented during the vessel’s 2022 field season, when the team explored deep-ocean environments and used remotely operated and autonomous systems to investigate remote and poorly surveyed areas.Right-angled cracks gave the formation its unusual appearanceThe report explains that the formation likely consists of hyaloclastite. This rock forms when hot magma comes into contact with cold water, causing volcanic material to break into fragments. Scientists said the surface likely represents fractured hyaloclastite, rather than a constructed pathway.The cracks intersect at right angles, producing the unusually neat pattern that gives the site its road-like appearance. The geometry may look carefully arranged, but it is part of the rock’s natural structure. The report attributes the formation to volcanic activity on the seafloor. The report says the formation is natural, not human-made.How did volcanic glass develop its yellowish appearanceThe yellow appearance also has a natural explanation. According to the report, the colour likely developed through low-temperature hydrothermal alteration of the volcanic glass. This process changes the material after it forms, leaving iron oxyhydroxide that gives the surface its yellowish colour. Hydrothermal alteration refers to changes caused when heated fluids interact with rock. In this case, the report presents it as the likely reason for the colour. Together, the fractured rock, right-angled cracks and altered volcanic glass give the seafloor feature the appearance of a road, although it was formed through natural geological activity in the area.The 2022 field season documented several other deep-sea discoveriesThe yellow brick road was one finding from the 2022 field season aboard E/V Nautilus. The report describes a wider programme of seafloor mapping, remotely operated vehicle dives and work with autonomous systems. It records 120 uncrewed vehicle deployments during the season. The expeditions also documented deep-sea coral and sponge communities, fossilised whale bones and a fossilised Megalodon tooth.Researchers observed and collected a sea pen from the genus Solumbellula, marking its first recorded observation and collection in the Pacific, according to the report. The work combined exploration with scientific research and public outreach, allowing people on shore to follow discoveries through live broadcasts and ship-to-shore connections during the same field season.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Madagascar's giant flying foxes have become smaller over four decades; researchers found their skulls are around 6% smaller than those collected before the 1980s, raising concerns about hunting pressure
articles.summary: One of Madagascar’s largest bat species is showing a striking physical change, with researchers finding that its skulls have become approximately 6 per
articles.body: One of Madagascar’s largest bat species is showing a striking physical change, with researchers finding that its skulls have become approximately 6 per cent smaller over the past four decades. The findings, published in the Journal of Mammalogy on October 29, 2026, point towards a possible connection between shrinking body size and increased hunting pressure. The research, also reported by Science News and conservation-focused publications, raises fresh questions about how human activity is changing wildlife populations and threatening species already facing population decline. The Malagasy flying fox (Pteropus rufus), known for its impressive wingspan and fox-like facial features, is among the world's largest bats. Found across Madagascar, these fruit-eating mammals play an important ecological role by dispersing seeds and helping maintain forest ecosystems. The research was led by Emily Cornelius Ruhs and Steven Goodman of Chicago's Field Museum. To investigate the apparent change, the scientists examined 121 preserved specimens held in nine natural history museums across the United States and Europe. The specimens represented more than 150 years of the species' history. The team recorded measurements of 12 different features of the bats' skulls and teeth. Their analysis revealed that specimens collected before the 1980s had skulls that were, on average, 3.6 millimetres longer than those collected in subsequent decades. This represents a difference of approximately 6 per cent.Why hunting could be changing their sizeResearchers believe the timing of the physical change may be significant. Until the 1980s, flying foxes were largely hunted on a small scale to provide food for individual families and local communities. However, hunting gradually became more commercialised, with bats increasingly being sold in markets and served in restaurants.The researchers suspect that larger bats may have become easier targets because of their size and the greater amount of meat they provide. This could have resulted in disproportionate hunting of larger individuals, gradually changing the physical characteristics seen in subsequent generations. A report by Mongabay also highlighted the importance of the species as a food source in Madagascar, where flying foxes are hunted for both household consumption and commercial sale. Some hunters use nets, while others shoot the animals before selling them.However, hunting is not necessarily the only explanation. The researchers have also identified deforestation, changing climatic conditions and shifts in fruit availability as possible contributors. The study establishes a strong association between the increase in commercial hunting and the decline in skull size, but does not conclusively establish that hunting alone caused the change.A shrinking species faces wider conservation concernsThe findings are particularly concerning because Malagasy flying foxes are already facing pressure from multiple directions. Beyond their role as a food source, the bats are important seed dispersers and pollinators. By feeding on fruits and nectar and moving between trees, they help support forest regeneration and maintain Madagascar's biodiversity. Their slow reproductive rate makes the situation more complicated. The loss of larger, sexually mature individuals could potentially affect the population's ability to reproduce and recover from continued hunting pressure.A study of this kind also highlights why museum collections are valuable to conservation science. Preserved specimens offer researchers a rare opportunity to compare wildlife across generations and identify physical changes that might otherwise go unnoticed. The researchers believe further monitoring and stronger protection, particularly around breeding sites, will be important to safeguard the species. They also want to understand whether similar physical changes are occurring in other fruit bats hunted across Madagascar. The findings offer a reminder that human activity can leave lasting effects on wildlife, sometimes in ways that become visible only after decades of change.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Scientists scooped 11 endangered alpine spiny crayfish from a Victorian creek after bushfires in January, keeping the feisty creatures apart in a hatchery; months later, they are being returned to their home waters
articles.summary: Bushfires can threaten to wipe out an entire wildlife species, let alone one that is already endangered.
articles.body: Bushfires can threaten to wipe out an entire wildlife species, let alone one that is already endangered. This is a concern that has prompted many conservationists and scientists to take part in rescue operations. In Victoria, Australia, a group of scientists rushed to the rescue of the endangered alpine spiny crayfish during the January 2026 bushfires, rescuing a total of 11 from a creek. Months later, after being cared for in captivity, the creatures are finally making their way back to the waters they call home.According to an ABC News report dated November 7, 2026, scientists from the Arthur Rylah Institute rescued 11 of these crayfish from a creek near Lucyvale in the immediate aftermath of the fires. The concern was that the creatures could suffocate as debris and sediment entered the waterway, affecting the conditions they depended on to survive. Will Sowersby, a senior scientist at the Arthur Rylah Institute, explained to ABC News that without intervention, the species could disappear from some of these freshwater areas. The rescue was therefore not simply about moving a handful of creatures away from an immediate threat, but also about protecting a vulnerable population whose limited distribution makes it particularly susceptible to environmental disturbances.The feisty residents of a conservation hatcheryOnce rescued, the 11 crayfish were transported to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery near Eildon, which is operated by the Victorian Fisheries Authority. They remained there while scientists waited for the water quality in their natural habitat to improve sufficiently for their return.However, keeping them alive in captivity presented an entirely different set of challenges. This was the first time alpine spiny crayfish had been taken into captivity, meaning hatchery staff were learning about their behaviour and care requirements as they went along. One of the more unexpected difficulties was just how aggressive the creatures could be towards one another. Dylan White, a senior conservation hatchery officer at Snobs Creek, told ABC News that the crayfish had to be housed separately because they would attack each other if kept together.It meant that the hatchery team had to make individual arrangements for the rescued animals, keeping them apart throughout their stay. While the creatures were no longer facing the immediate threat of deteriorating water conditions in the creek, their temporary home still required careful attention to ensure they remained healthy until they could be returned.Preparing for a future beyond the rescueThe return of the crayfish comes as the Victorian High Country gradually recovers from the Walwa-River Road bushfire, which burned approximately 121,000 hectares. Although the immediate danger has passed for the rescued animals, scientists are continuing to monitor the waterways and the surrounding habitat to understand how the species will fare in the months ahead.There is also a larger conservation question emerging from the experience. Scientists hope that alpine spiny crayfish could eventually become part of a captive breeding programme at the Snobs Creek hatchery. The hatchery itself has become an important centre for the rescue and care of vulnerable freshwater species following natural disasters. Its staff have also looked after other animals affected by Victoria's summer bushfires, including Macquarie perch and trout cod rescued from Seven Creek following the Longwood bushfire. More than 100 of these fish have already been released back into the wild. However, the work at the hatchery is not without its challenges for the staff, as each rescue brings a different set of requirements and, sometimes, the need to learn how to care for a species that has never been kept in captivity before.For the alpine spiny crayfish, the journey from a fire-affected creek to a conservation hatchery and eventually back to their home waters has been an atypical one. Their rescue also offers a reminder that the consequences of a bushfire are not always immediately visible. Beneath the surface of a stream, entire populations of small and often overlooked creatures can be at risk, making the work of protecting them just as important as restoring the landscapes we see above ground. With the country at risk of facing more natural disasters as climate change progresses, protection and rescue operations for species, particularly those already at a high risk of extinction, have become a need of the hour.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Researchers tracking endangered Carnaby's cockatoos in Western Australia found that tiny patches of surviving bushland act as stepping stones across cleared farms, showing why even fragments of native habitat matter
articles.summary: Habitat loss is one of the most devastating consequences of rapid urbanisation and human expansion.
articles.body: Habitat loss is one of the most devastating consequences of rapid urbanisation and human expansion. As forests are cleared to make room for farms, roads and buildings, animals are left with fewer places to find food, water and shelter. And while we often imagine conservation as protecting vast stretches of untouched wilderness, sometimes, even a small patch of greenery can make a world of difference.Researchers tracking endangered Carnaby’s cockatoos in Western Australia have discovered just how important these overlooked pockets of nature can be. Their study found that tiny fragments of surviving native bushland act as stepping stones, helping the birds move between larger patches of habitat in landscapes that have been heavily cleared for agriculture. It is a reminder that when it comes to protecting wildlife, every little bit of nature counts.What did the researchers find?A team from Murdoch University's Harry Butler Institute, led by Dr Jill Shephard and Dr Zoë Kissane, wanted to understand how habitat loss and fragmentation affected the movement of Carnaby’s cockatoos during their breeding season.The researchers fitted GPS satellite tracking devices to 18 wild cockatoos across five inland breeding sites in Western Australia's Wheatbelt region. They then monitored the birds' movements throughout the breeding season to understand how far they travelled to find food and how the surrounding landscape influenced their journeys.The findings revealed a rather worrying difference. Birds living in heavily fragmented landscapes had to travel roughly three times farther each day to find food than those in areas where native vegetation remained relatively connected.At Coomallo, where much of the surrounding bushland had been cleared, the cockatoos travelled an average of more than 37 kilometres every day in search of food. At Tenterden, where the vegetation was more connected, they travelled just over 10 kilometres.Think about what that means for a bird that already has to spend a considerable part of its day finding enough food to survive. Longer journeys require more time and energy, leaving less room for other essential activities, including breeding and raising chicks. Researchers warn that this additional pressure could eventually affect the birds' breeding success and the ability of their populations to survive.However, the most interesting discovery was not simply how far the cockatoos were travelling. It was where they were stopping along the way.Even small, degraded patches of native vegetation, which might otherwise look insignificant in an agricultural landscape, were being used by the birds. These fragments acted as stepping stones, allowing cockatoos to move between larger areas of suitable habitat rather than having to cross vast stretches of cleared land.This is particularly important because conservation efforts have traditionally prioritised large, healthy patches of forest and woodland. While protecting these areas remains essential, the research suggests that smaller remnants deserve attention too.The researchers also raised concerns about existing land-clearing guidelines. Under Australia's federal Black Cockatoo Referral Guidelines, clearing less than one hectare of foraging habitat or less than 10 hectares of low-quality habitat is unlikely to require referral to the government regulator. However, the study found that Carnaby's cockatoos regularly used patches considerably smaller than these thresholds. This suggests that the current guidelines may underestimate the importance of smaller areas of native vegetation.A little about Carnaby's cockatoosNative to south-western Western Australia, Carnaby's cockatoos (Zanda latirostris), also known as short-billed black cockatoos, are large, striking birds recognised by their black plumage, white tail bands and distinctive calls. They can grow up to 58 centimetres long and are highly social, often travelling and feeding in pairs or flocks.These birds have a rather particular relationship with their surroundings. They feed on the seeds of native plants such as Banksia, Marri, Jarrah and Hakea, along with nectar, flowers and insect larvae. They also depend on old eucalyptus trees for nesting. In fact, these trees need to be more than 100 years old to develop hollows large enough to accommodate their nests.Carnaby's cockatoos generally breed between July and December, often returning to the same breeding areas year after year. They also tend to mate for life, making the availability of suitable nesting sites and nearby food sources particularly important.Unfortunately, habitat destruction has put these beautiful birds under considerable pressure. Agricultural expansion and urban development have removed large areas of their natural feeding and breeding grounds. According to the University of Western Australia, the species has lost more than half its population over the past 45 years.The problem is not just that there are fewer trees. The remaining trees and patches of vegetation are increasingly isolated from one another, making it harder for the birds to find food and reach suitable nesting areas.Why every little patch of green mattersThe findings come at a time when conservationists are looking for ways to reconnect fragmented landscapes. In June 2026, the University of Western Australia announced the Corridors for Carnaby's project, an initiative that aims to restore 1,000 hectares of habitat by planting more than 200,000 trees along a 10-kilometre stretch of land south of Mandurah. The project also plans to install artificial nesting sites and water stations to support the birds.While large-scale restoration projects are important, the latest research highlights something that is easy to overlook: protecting what already exists is just as important as planting something new.A small patch of woodland might not look like much when surrounded by acres of farmland. It might not even resemble a forest worth saving. But for a hungry cockatoo travelling across an increasingly unfamiliar landscape, it could be the place where it finds its next meal, takes a break or safely continues its journey.Habitat loss is not always about a forest disappearing overnight. Sometimes, it happens gradually, one tree and one patch of vegetation at a time, until the spaces between surviving habitats become too large to cross.We often measure the value of nature by how much land it occupies. Perhaps it is time we also consider how much life it supports. After all, for an animal trying to survive in a world that is steadily shrinking around it, even the smallest patch of green can be a lifeline.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns from orbit and is captured by launch pad arms in a dramatic first
articles.summary: (AP) — SpaceX’s Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.It...
articles.body:
CAPE CANAVERAL, Fla. (AP) — SpaceX's Starship made a triumphant return to Earth on Saturday, caught in midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

It was the grand finale that Elon Musk and his team hoped for — the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space. But with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday's liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch, still the goal for accelerating moon and Mars travel.

Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys, as the stainless steel, bullet-shaped spacecraft lowered itself upright at the launch pad.

The dramatic, sci-fi-like capture helped blot out the booster's messy miss. Cameras panned the spacecraft up and down as it hung high above the ground, supported by the arms of the launch tower.

"Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot shouted, dragging out each word. "Look at her! Baby, she's back!"

Calling it an "epic day," Musk later ascended the launch tower to take up-close video with his phone. He even hugged the spacecraft. "Looks great," he reported via X.

SpaceX officials said Saturday's catch demonstrates the full reusability of Starship, crucial for rapid and low-cost recycling. Although Friday's booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA welcomed Saturday's news. The space agency is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the moon later this decade and help build a permanent lunar base. Musk's ambitions are even grander: He wants to launch a fleet of Starships to build a city on Mars.

"It was almost magic," NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said via X. "Making more believers by the day ... one step closer to (emojis of the moon and the U.S. flag)."

The world's largest and most powerful rocket — a 407-foot (124-meter) behemoth — blasted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starship base near the U.S.-Mexican border. Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

Starship continued circling the world 165 miles (265 kilometers) up, with live views of itself and Earth streaming down via Starlink. The spacecraft completed 14 laps around Earth, outshining the previous mission's one to two laps.

It was SpaceX's 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

As for the booster, SpaceX's Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster's guidance system sensed it wasn't in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months. That is the starting point for NASA's next Artemis mission, which will skip the moon and remain in orbit around Earth for lunar lander practice.

Artemis III's four astronauts will attempt to dock their capsule with not only Starship but Blue Origin's Blue Moon. The two companies will take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface. NASA is targeting as soon as 2028 for Artemis IV, humanity's first moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.

articles.summary: SpaceX captured Starship using the arms of ‘Mechazilla’ its launch and catch tower for the first time.
articles.body: After aborting a planned catch of Starship Flight 15’s booster, SpaceX successfully captured Starship with its “Mechazilla” launch and catch tower for the first time. The company has performed ‘chopstick’ catches of its boosters before, but this is the first time the maneuver has successfully been executed on the Starship vehicle itself. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said during the company’s third-quarter earnings call that “success is not guaranteed on these first flights, but I’d say it’s more likely than not that this succeeds next flight.” While not a complete success, in that the company was unable to recover the entire launch vehicle, it still stands as a milestone for the Starship program. And, since it has previously caught boosters on previous launches, there is reason to believe the failure today was not an insurmountable obstacle. SpaceX is still trying to determine what caused the booster to abort its landing and detonate over the Gulf of Mexico. articles.title: Two infants were buried together in a ceramic urn in Peru about 1,600 years ago; one had a single central eye socket, and scientists have now used ancient DNA to identify the genetic condition behind it
articles.summary: We often look back in time through the eyes of the victors, the rulers and the elite.
articles.body: We often look back in time through the eyes of the victors, the rulers and the elite. Even in their funerals, they are commemorated as such so we learn a lot about them. Sometimes, we learn about the past through ordinary men and women, discovering their stories and lives.Rarely do we find stories from babies. Their lives are often too brief to leave behind much of a historical record, and their remains can tell us only so much. In southern Peru, archaeologists discovered the remains of two infants buried together in a ceramic vessel. One of them had a single eye socket in the centre of her face, a rare congenital condition known as cyclopia. Now, researchers have used ancient DNA to identify the genetic condition behind it, revealing an extraordinary piece of the history of human development.The discovery, published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), offers a rare opportunity to understand a congenital condition that has left little evidence in the archaeological record. It also raises questions about the lives of two infants who were laid to rest together more than 1,600 years ago.Two infants, one burialThe remains were discovered at Jauranga, an archaeological site in Peru's Palpa Valley, a region associated with the ancient Nasca civilisation. The burial dates to the Middle Nasca period, between AD 325 and 440.Inside a single ceramic vessel, researchers found the remains of two infants, placed one above the other. The skeletons were preserved in their natural positions, suggesting that they had been buried together in a single event.The infant at the bottom, identified as JA13A, had several unusual skeletal features. Her skull had a single eye socket positioned along the centre of her face, rather than the two separate sockets typically found in humans. The second infant, JA13B, did not show comparable skeletal abnormalities.Genetic analysis revealed that both infants were female, but they did not share the same maternal lineage. This means they were not biological sisters through their mother's side, although their precise relationship, if any, remains unknown.Why the two children were buried together is another question researchers have not been able to answer. While placing young children in ceramic vessels was an established funerary practice in the region, burying two infants in the same vessel was unusual.Understanding cyclopiaCyclopia is an extremely rare congenital condition associated with a severe form of a developmental disorder called holoprosencephaly.During early pregnancy, the developing brain is supposed to divide into two hemispheres. In holoprosencephaly, this separation does not happen completely. In its most severe form, the condition can affect the development of the brain and face, preventing the two eye sockets from forming separately.Instead, the infant may develop a single eye socket positioned in the middle of the face. The condition can also affect the development of the nose, upper jaw and other facial structures.Cyclopia is typically fatal before or shortly after birth. It is estimated to occur in approximately one in 100,000 births, although the actual number of affected pregnancies is difficult to establish because many do not progress to birth.While the unusual structure of JA13A's skull helped researchers identify the condition, they wanted to understand what had caused it. This is where modern genetic technology came into the picture.Ancient DNA uncovers the genetic explanationResearchers extracted ancient DNA from the infant's remains to investigate the possible cause of her condition. Their analysis revealed that JA13A had an extra copy of chromosome 13, a genetic condition known as trisomy 13, or Patau syndrome.Most people have two copies of each chromosome. In individuals with trisomy 13, there are three copies of chromosome 13 instead. This additional genetic material can interfere with normal development, causing a range of congenital conditions affecting the brain, heart, face and other parts of the body.Cyclopia is one of the possible manifestations of trisomy 13, although it occurs in only a small proportion of affected individuals. The researchers identified the chromosomal abnormality as the likely cause of the infant's condition.This is particularly significant because the discovery is believed to be the first known archaeological example of cyclopia identified in human skeletal remains. While the condition has been documented in modern medical collections, finding evidence of it in an ancient burial is considerably rarer.The researchers also examined the infants' skeletal development to understand their ages. Interestingly, the teeth and limb bones suggested slightly different developmental timelines, making it difficult to establish precisely how long JA13A survived. The findings suggest that she may have lived beyond birth, but her exact lifespan remains uncertain.A glimpse into the Nasca communityBeyond the medical discovery, the burial offers an interesting glimpse into how the Nasca community may have treated children with congenital differences.The infant with cyclopia was buried in a ceramic vessel, a practice commonly associated with young children in the region. Her grave was located in a regular cemetery and did not contain unusual offerings that suggested she had received a distinctly different funerary treatment.Researchers believe this could indicate that her condition did not lead to her being excluded from customary burial practices. However, a burial can only tell us so much. It cannot establish how she was treated during her life, whether she received care or what her community thought about her condition.Nor can one discovery explain how an entire civilisation viewed people with disabilities.Still, the findings offer a valuable reminder that congenital differences have always been part of human history, even when they have rarely survived in the archaeological record.More than 1,600 years after two infants were laid to rest together, scientists have managed to uncover a genetic explanation for one child's condition. We may never know their names, why they shared a burial or what their brief lives looked like. But their remains have given researchers an opportunity to understand a rare condition that would otherwise have remained hidden in the past.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: In 2024, New Jersey began restoring a 290-acre marsh and former industrial site by excavating tidal channels and building bird islands; by 2026, ospreys, bald eagles and herons were using the habitat
articles.summary: In New Jersey, a restoration project at Higbee Beach Wildlife Management Area is bringing back the natural function of a coastal marsh that human activity
articles.body: In New Jersey, a restoration project at Higbee Beach Wildlife Management Area is bringing back the natural function of a coastal marsh that human activity had previously impacted.The project, which began in February 2024, covers a 290-acre section of the wildlife management area in Cape May County and includes Pond Creek marsh, Davey's Lake and land occupied by a former magnesite manufacturing facility and its associated landfill. Two years into the restoration, the changes are already conspicuous, with ospreys, bald eagles, great blue herons and several other bird species observed using the newly built waterbodies.According to the New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection's Spring 2026 project update, the restoration is being led by its Office of Natural Resource Restoration and Office of Coastal Engineering, in partnership with the state's Division of Fish and Wildlife. The primary objective is to restore tidal movement through much of Pond Creek marsh, which had been affected by earlier modifications to the landscape.The former Harbison-Walker Magnesite facility had a considerable influence on the surrounding area. The plant extracted magnesium from seawater, and historical changes to the site interrupted the natural tidal connection between Pond Creek marsh and Delaware Bay. With the movement of water restricted, parts of the marsh became degraded and were increasingly dominated by non-native common reed, known as Phragmites australis.As seawater moves into and out of a marsh, it influences the distribution of nutrients, the availability of water and the habitats that different species depend upon. The restoration team began work in February 2024, initially preparing the site, clearing vegetation and installing measures to control soil erosion and sediment movement. A temporary ditch plug was also constructed to disconnect tidal flow into Pond Creek while the initial construction work was carried out.Creating new channels and islandsExcavating channels to restore tidal flow has been the most crucial part of this project. Rather than simply reopening the existing waterway, the restoration design includes a wider main channel, along with a network of smaller channels that will help water move through the interior of the wetland.The excavation of the main channel, extending approximately 3,561 feet, was completed in November 2024. By November 2025, the interior tributaries, measuring approximately 14,220 feet in total, and additional pond features had also been excavated. The work generated around 148,591 cubic yards of material, which could be reused elsewhere within the restoration site.This excavated material has played another important role in reshaping the landscape. Instead of treating all the removed soil as waste, the project has reused it to construct elevated areas and habitat features within the marsh.Five sand-shell habitat islands were completed in August 2025. Located in open sections of the marsh, these islands are intended to provide nesting and feeding areas for migratory birds. The restoration has also involved creating high marsh areas, mudflats and open-water habitats, offering a wider variety of conditions for wildlife to use.The project has not been limited to the wetland itself. Several dune systems have also been constructed and planted with native beachgrass, Ammophila breviligulata, while panic grass (Panicum amarum) has been used for seeding. These plantings help establish coastal vegetation and contribute to the restoration of the surrounding upland habitat.Wildlife is already making use of the changesPerhaps the most encouraging development has been the wildlife recorded at the site while construction is still underway. The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection's Spring 2026 update notes that aquatic prey species, including mummichogs, have been found in the newly constructed waterbodies. Their presence has attracted a variety of birds, including ospreys, great blue herons and bald eagles, along with egrets, kingfishers and gulls.The presence of these birds is particularly important given that the project is situated in Cape May, an important stopover along the Atlantic Flyway. This peninsula is internationally recognised for its seasonal bird migrations, with large numbers of birds passing through as they travel between their breeding and wintering grounds. The restored marsh is therefore expected to provide feeding and resting habitats for several species, including raptors such as peregrine falcons, merlins and kestrels. Apart from birds, the department has also recorded other wildlife using the site, including snakes, raccoons, foxes, otters and beavers.The project has also incorporated 26 dead trees, known as tree snags, into the landscape. These were sourced from the site itself and installed along and within the newly excavated tributaries. Although they may appear like remnants of a damaged landscape, dead trees can provide useful resting and feeding places for birds, while those placed in waterways can also offer habitat for fish.A restoration that goes beyond wildlifeRestoring tidal movement needs to be balanced with protecting freshwater habitats and reducing the risk of flooding in the surrounding watershed. To address this concern, the project includes an earthen berm system fitted with water-control structures that can regulate tidal inundation in specific areas, helping protect freshwater habitats while allowing tidal movement to be restored across the marsh.The restoration also aims to improve public access to the landscape through trails, boardwalks, viewing platforms and bird observation structures. According to the Spring 2026 update, construction of several recreational features, including the heron canopy, pedestrian bridge, boardwalks and viewing blinds, was completed during Summer 2026, with some additional work still underway. The installation of pedestrian benches and interpretive signs along the trails is also forthcoming.By rebuilding tidal connections, creating new habitats and allowing native vegetation to establish itself, New Jersey is working towards a landscape where wildlife can once again find the resources it needs.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship captured by launchpad arms in dramatic first
articles.summary: SpaceX officials say catch by mechanical arms shows Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.
articles.body:
SpaceX’s Starship ‌spacecraft has returned to Earth, caught midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky on Saturday, descending slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 in Texas – the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.

Soon afterwards, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk congratulated his “incredible team”.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.

However, with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it was not in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon later this decade, welcomed the achievement.

“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.

Starship completed 14 laps around the Earth, 265km (165 miles), outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

Starship, a 124-metre (407ft) behemoth, is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for Moon and Mars travel.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.
