articles.title: A bronze leg found in a Scottish bog in 1820 was thought to be stolen Roman loot; researchers now believe it belonged to a giant gilded statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius
articles.summary: Antoninus Pius was a Roman emperor, specifically the fourth of the Five Good Emperors, who ruled from AD 138 to 161.
articles.body: Antoninus Pius was a Roman emperor, specifically the fourth of the Five Good Emperors, who ruled from AD 138 to 161. His reign was marked by relative peace and stability across the Roman Empire, alongside administrative and legal reforms. However, one of his more ambitious undertakings was expanding Rome's territory further north into Scotland, a campaign that resulted in the construction of the Antonine Wall.The emperor's legacy was not limited to the territories he conquered or the policies he introduced. Like many Roman rulers, Antoninus Pius also had monuments and statues erected in his honour, celebrating his achievements and reinforcing his authority across the empire. One such monument may have been a towering, gilded bronze statue of the emperor riding a horse, which is believed to have once stood in southern Scotland.But if the Romans had gone to such lengths to immortalise their emperor, why was the statue eventually taken apart? A bronze leg discovered in a Scottish bog more than 200 years ago may finally offer some answers. Ahead of the Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire, an exhibition at the National Museum of Scotland, the museum has released a statement regarding the same. Once thought to have been stolen by Scottish tribes from a Roman settlement further south, the artefact is now believed to have been deliberately removed by Roman soldiers themselves.A glimpse of an emperor's lost monumentThe bronze leg, now known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog near Hawick, in the Scottish Borders, in 1820. It is a larger-than-life lower right leg, complete with a boot, made from bronze and originally covered in gold. Dating back to around AD 140, it is believed to be the only surviving fragment of a monumental Roman imperial statue ever discovered in Scotland.For more than 200 years, however, its origins were understood quite differently. The prevailing theory was that the fragment had been stolen from a Roman settlement further south, possibly York, and carried into Scotland by local tribes. It was difficult for historians to imagine that the Romans would have erected such an elaborate monument so far north of their established frontier.Recent research has challenged this assumption. By studying the fragment alongside other Roman statues found in frontier regions, archaeologists at National Museums Scotland believe it may have belonged to a colossal equestrian statue of Antoninus Pius. In other words, the emperor was probably depicted sitting on horseback, much like the famous bronze statue of Marcus Aurelius that still stands in Rome.The surviving leg offers a few clues about what the original sculpture looked like. Its upper edge remains intact, with no visible signs of having been hacked or sawn off. There is also an interesting detail around the knee: the bronze is not gilded in this area, suggesting that it was originally concealed beneath the emperor's tunic or cloak. The rest of the statue, including the emperor's torso and the horse, has yet to be found.Researchers have even created a full-scale reconstruction of the proposed monument, using the surviving leg to give visitors an idea of its original grandeur. It would have been quite a sight in Roman Scotland, particularly for the local Iron Age communities. According to Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, naturalistic human portraiture was relatively unfamiliar in the region. A towering, gold-covered emperor on horseback would have been an unmistakable display of Roman power.The statue was likely commissioned to commemorate Antoninus Pius's victories in Scotland during the 140s AD. Its placement in the newly occupied territory would have served a purpose beyond decoration. It was a way of making Rome's presence visible, reminding local communities who controlled the land and celebrating the emperor responsible for its expansion.Why were Roman statues stolen in the first place?The assumption that the Milsington leg had been stolen was not entirely far-fetched. Roman statues were valuable objects, particularly those made from bronze and covered in gold. Their worth extended beyond their artistic craftsmanship. Bronze could be melted down and reused to make weapons, tools, coins and other objects, making large sculptures attractive sources of raw material. In territories where Roman control was contested, monuments could also become targets during conflicts, with defeated communities dismantling symbols of the power that had ruled over them.There was also a political reason why statues of emperors were sometimes destroyed. Roman rulers were closely associated with their public image, and their likenesses appeared across cities, military settlements and conquered territories. When an emperor was disgraced or declared an enemy of the state, authorities could order his images and inscriptions to be removed. This practice, commonly referred to as damnatio memoriae, was an attempt to erase his public legacy. Statues could be damaged, dismantled or repurposed, depending on the circumstances.This is partly why the discovery of the Milsington leg is so interesting. If it had been violently looted, researchers might have expected to find signs of rough removal. Instead, its intact upper edge suggests that it was carefully separated from the rest of the monument. The absence of damage changes the story considerably.Archaeologists now believe that Roman soldiers themselves may have dismantled the statue when they withdrew from southern Scotland. Following Antoninus Pius's death in AD 161, Roman forces eventually abandoned the Antonine Wall and retreated towards Hadrian's Wall. Rather than leave valuable monuments behind for local communities or rival forces to claim, they may have deliberately taken them apart and buried their components.There is evidence of similar practices elsewhere along the frontier. Roman forces dismantled and buried important monuments, including stone altars and inscriptions associated with the Antonine Wall, rather than simply abandoning them. The Milsington leg may have been treated in much the same way.Why this particular fragment was left behind, while the rest of the sculpture disappeared, remains unclear. Some pieces may have been transported elsewhere, while others could have been melted down and reused. It is also possible that more fragments are still buried in the surrounding landscape. For now, the bronze leg is a reminder that even an empire as powerful as Rome did not always leave its monuments standing when it moved on.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Watch: SpaceX's Starship completes first-ever midair catch on return from orbit
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from a 22-hour journey in orbit on Saturday and was caught by giant mechanical arms at the Texas launch tower from
articles.body: SpaceX's Starship spacecraft returned from a 22-hour journey in orbit on Saturday and was caught by giant mechanical arms at the Texas launch tower from which it had taken off a day earlier, marking the first successful recovery of the spacecraft in midair.The dramatic landing was a major milestone in Elon Musk's effort to develop a fully reusable rocket system. However, SpaceX fell short of its goal of recovering both stages of the rocket after the Super Heavy booster exploded shortly after Friday's launch.The stainless steel spacecraft descended through clouds over SpaceX's Starbase facility, reignited its engines to turn upright and slowly lowered itself into the launch tower's mechanical arms, known as Mechazilla.Its engines shut down after the catch, leaving the charred spacecraft suspended above the ground.SpaceX shared a video of the historic landing, showing Starship descending towards the launch tower before being caught by its giant mechanical arms. The spacecraft was seen settling into the arms and remaining suspended above the ground after its engines shut down.Sharing the footage, SpaceX wrote: "Mechazilla catches Starship! Congratulations to the entire SpaceX team on this incredible achievement!""Can you believe it?" SpaceX commentator Dan Huot exclaimed during the broadcast. "Look at her! Baby, she's back!"Musk congratulated his team after the successful recovery, while SpaceX officials said the achievement demonstrated the potential for Starship's full reusability, which is central to the company's plans for faster and lower-cost space travel.Nasa administrator Jared Isaacman also welcomed the development. "It was almost magic," he said in a post on X, adding that the achievement was making "more believers by the day".Starship completes 14 orbits and deploys 26 satellitesThe 407-foot (124-metre) rocket lifted off late Friday afternoon from SpaceX's Starbase facility in Texas, near the US-Mexico border. Its two stages separated successfully, allowing the upper-stage Starship spacecraft to continue towards orbit.During the mission, Starship deployed 26 advanced Starlink satellites before continuing to circle Earth at an altitude of around 161-165 miles (260-265 kilometres). It completed 14 orbits over more than 22 hours, a significant increase from the one to two laps completed during the previous mission.The flight was SpaceX's 15th full-scale Starship mission since 2023 and only its second trip to orbit. The company said the spacecraft's systems, including its heat shield, appeared to have worked well.Starship began its return by firing an engine to initiate its descent into the atmosphere.Travelling at an orbital speed of around 17,000 miles per hour, it faced intense heat as it slowed during re-entry before reaching the launch site.The Super Heavy booster, which carried the spacecraft into space, failed to complete its own recovery attempt around 10 minutes after liftoff. SpaceX official Kate Tice said the booster's engines had stopped firing too early during its return.Its guidance system detected that it was not in the correct position and automatically initiated a diversion towards the water, followed by the booster's destruction. Engineers are investigating the cause of the failure. Wreckage remained in the Gulf of Mexico, cordoned off by buoys.Full reusability remains a work in progressWhile Saturday's successful catch marked a key step towards recovering Starship, SpaceX has yet to retrieve both stages of the rocket in the same mission. The spacecraft's heat shield, made up of black hexagonal tiles designed to withstand the extreme temperatures of atmospheric re-entry, is also not yet fully reusable, Reuters reported.The company is developing new tile designs that would require little or no refurbishment between flights.SpaceX's existing Falcon 9 rocket has a reusable first stage and has completed more than 700 launches since 2010. Its second stage, which carries payloads into orbit, is discarded into the ocean after each flight.Musk wants Starship to operate more like a commercial aircraft, travelling to space and returning for repeated flights with minimal refurbishment. The system is expected to support the company's Starlink satellite business, as well as its ambitions involving orbital data centres, lunar exploration and eventual human settlement on Mars.Starship central to Nasa's Artemis moon programmeNasa is also relying on Starship for its lunar exploration plans, paying billions of dollars for the spacecraft to serve as a lunar lander for Artemis astronauts later this decade and support the development of a permanent base on the Moon.SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida's Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.The facility is expected to be the starting point for Nasa's next Artemis mission, which will remain in orbit around Earth rather than travel to the Moon, allowing astronauts to practise lunar lander operations.For Artemis III, four astronauts are expected to attempt to dock their capsule with both SpaceX's Starship and Blue Origin's Blue Moon lunar lander. The two companies are expected to take turns delivering crews to the lunar surface.Nasa is targeting 2028 for Artemis IV, which aims to achieve humanity's first Moon landing since the Apollo era more than half a century ago.The successful recovery also comes as SpaceX continues to develop Starship for Musk's longer-term ambition of sending a fleet of spacecraft to Mars and building a city there.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: A 4,000-year-old jug in Turkey holds seeds of a rare flower found nowhere else on Earth; but its survival is at risk
articles.summary: Archaeologists working at Külhöyük, a mound in Ankara’s Gölbaşı district, have discovered the oldest known seed remains of Turkey's rare 'love flower'
articles.body: Archaeologists working at Külhöyük, a mound in Ankara’s Gölbaşı district, have discovered the oldest known seed remains of Turkey's rare 'love flower' inside a Hittite jug dating back approximately 4,000 years. The discovery, announced by Culture and Tourism Minister Mehmet Nuri Ersoy in September 2026, offers evidence that the distinctive flower has existed in the region since the Bronze Age. However, the plant, known to botanists as *Centaurea tchihatcheffii*, is now critically endangered, and its survival may depend partly on how and when farmers cultivate the fields where it grows.Locally called 'sevgi çiçeği', the flower is found naturally only in the Gölbaşı area around Ankara, making it an endemic species with a highly restricted geographical range. Turkish conservation authorities classify it as critically endangered. The excavation was directed by Derya Yilmaz Tekin of Ankara University, whose report on the 2024 excavation season provided details about the unusual discovery.According to Tekin, the jug is a nearly complete piece of coarse pottery with a rounded body. Three small knobs sit on its shoulder, while its handle and rim are broken. It was discovered in Room 1 of a large building at the centre of the archaeological mound. The room also contained the base of a storage vessel, weaving weights made from broken pottery, a piece of an obsidian blade and a damaged mud-brick hearth.Other objects recovered from the same building included fragments of bull-headed cult bowls and unfinished seals. Tekin interpreted these findings as possible evidence of a seal cutter's workshop, with most of the discoveries dating to the beginning of the Old Hittite period.Archaeobotanists Emel Oybak-Dönmez and Barbaros Yaman examined the ancient plant remains recovered from the site. Their initial analysis of the 2024 material identified bread wheat, einkorn, barley, lentils and bitter vetch. Oak seeds and remains of the love flower also appeared in the site's second-millennium BC layers.The specialists identified the flower remains inside the jug as the oldest known seed material of the species. Tekin said the botanical evidence suggested that the plant had been present in the region since the Hittite period. However, researchers have not established why the seeds were placed inside the vessel or whether they were being stored for a particular purpose.Külhöyük is itself an important archaeological site. According to Ankara University, the mound measures approximately 820 feet in length, 490 feet in width and 72 feet in height. Settlement at the site began around the third millennium BC under the Hattians, before it developed into a Hittite city during the following millennium.The site came to archaeological attention in 1978 after illegal excavators exposed it. Museum teams subsequently conducted 14 seasons of rescue excavations between 1992 and 2006, uncovering massive stone city walls. Tekin has led the more recent excavation work since 2021, representing Ankara University and Turkey's Culture and Tourism Ministry.Despite having survived in the region for thousands of years, Centaurea tchihatcheffii faces several threats. The Turkish government's nature conservation directorate lists urban development, intensive farming, herbicide use and the burning of agricultural stubble among the pressures affecting the species. A 2008 doctoral study by Yasemin Ergüner Baytok at Middle East Technical University examined the plant's distribution and population trends. The researcher mapped 14 scattered subpopulations and monitored two of them between 2004 and 2008. One of the study's findings was particularly significant: herbicides emerged as the most serious human-related threat, causing high plant mortality and reducing seed germination. However, the research also found that cultivation practices could have a more complicated relationship with the flower's survival.Tillage, or the mechanical turning of agricultural soil, was found to increase plant density in the following year. Baytok's modelling suggested that delaying ploughing until after the plants had produced seeds could help populations remain viable. The study recommended ploughing protected patches after seed-setting, ideally once every two years.Authorities have already undertaken measures to protect the species. A conservation project around Lake Mogan began in 2016, involving fencing off growing areas, managing agricultural land, collecting seeds and sowing them in suitable locations. The flower also received geographical indication registration in 2019 through the Gölbaşı Municipality, recognising its association with the region. Its local name 'yanardöner' refers to its changing appearance under different light conditions. The annual plant belongs to the daisy family and produces flowers in red, pink, purple and whitish shades. Its flowering season generally runs from late April to early July.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Harvard scientist pushes back on NASA chief over mystery space object: 'It's not an asteroid'
articles.summary: Avi Loeb challenges NASA's Jared Isaacman, arguing 1998 KY26 is not an asteroid and could be a lost Soviet spacecraft from a failed Mars mission.
articles.body: A Harvard astrophysicist behind the theory that a mysterious object speeding through the solar system could actually be a lost Soviet spacecraft is pushing back on NASA's top official, saying the object is "not an asteroid." Known as 1998 KY26, the roughly 36-foot-wide object is believed to be a near-Earth asteroid but is accelerating in a way gravity alone cannot explain. Harvard astrophysicist Avi Loeb and his colleagues have examined whether it could instead be Phobos 1, a Soviet spacecraft that stopped communicating while traveling to Mars in 1988. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman weighed in on the mysterious object Thursday during an appearance on "Fox & Friends." EIFFEL TOWER-SIZED ASTEROID APOPHIS TO PASS CLOSER TO EARTH THAN MANY SATELLITES IN 2029, NASA SAYS "I've not seen any evidence to suggest this is...anything other than an asteroid," Isaacman said. Loeb challenged that assessment during an interview with Fox News Digital on Friday. HARVARD ASTRONOMER TAPPED TO LEAD WHITE HOUSE UFO COUNCIL SAYS US GOVERNMENT 'BAFFLED BY WHAT THEY ARE SEEING' "Well, first of all, it's not an asteroid because 1998 KY26 appears to have non-gravitational acceleration, meaning it's being pushed by some force other than gravity, and asteroids are just rocks," Loeb said. Scientists have been trying to explain what is causing the additional acceleration. SCIENTISTS DISCOVER POTENTIALLY MASSIVE DWARF PLANET CANDIDATE HIDING BEYOND PLUTO One theory has been that KY26 is a "dark comet," a rocky object behaving like a comet without producing a visible cloud or tail. New research from Georgia Tech has cast doubt on whether KY26 could retain enough ice to produce that effect, while other research has suggested pressure from sunlight and heat radiating from its surface could account for the acceleration. GIANT ROBOTIC CLAWS WILL GRAB DEAD SATELLITES IN SPACE Loeb told Fox News Digital that his team found KY26's trajectory closely resembles that of the failed Soviet mission and calculated that sunlight reflecting off Phobos 1 could produce a push consistent with the nongravitational acceleration observed in KY26. He also pointed to recent observations indicating the object is highly reflective and rotates about once every five minutes. NASA'S CHANDRA TELESCOPE REVEALS MILKY WAY'S OUTER REACHES MAY STRETCH FARTHER THAN PREVIOUSLY KNOWN The lack of a visible cometary tail or evidence of material escaping the object is central to Loeb's skepticism of the dark-comet explanation. "It could be a comet shedding some gas backward that is pushing it forward, but in that case we should have seen the gas," Loeb said. "We should have seen the dust because for comets we see a tail and the dust particles are being pushed away from the sun by the solar radiation." "We don't see a cometary tail. We don't see any evidence for outgassing around this object. That's the puzzle," he added. Loeb compared the debate over how to classify KY26 to encountering an unfamiliar animal at a zoo. FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X "If you are an expert on zebras and you see an elephant, you would say the elephant is a zebra without stripes," Loeb said. "But that's an oxymoron because it's a completely different animal." He also argued that scientists should be willing to consider explanations outside the familiar categories of asteroids and comets when observations do not neatly fit either one. THE NEXT FRONTIER: WASHINGTON GRAPPLES WITH ITS LATEST SPACE ODDITY "Innovation in science requires some imagination," Loeb said. "It requires you to allow for the possibility that our knowledge is incomplete." SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS Fox News Digital reached out to NASA for a response to Loeb's comments and asked whether Isaacman stands by his assessment of KY26. "In a paper published in 2025, NASA completed a comprehensive orbital analysis of near-Earth asteroid 1998 KY26 and concluded its behavior is driven by solar radiation forces," NASA told Fox News Digital. "Using recent measurements of the asteroid's shape, size, and rotation, a team led by NASA's Center for Near-Earth Object Studies determined that the asteroid's complex trajectory is due to solar radiation forces, which are the natural push of sunlight and thermal emission on its non-spherical shape. "This analysis demonstrates the asteroid's path isn't caused by hidden comet-like activity." CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB Loeb acknowledged that his team's theory remains unproven, but said a definitive answer could come in 2031, when the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's Hayabusa2 spacecraft is expected to rendezvous with KY26. SEND US A TIP Loeb predicts the encounter could show that scientists have been looking at a piece of Soviet space history rather than an unusual natural object. GOT A TIP? "We predict that when they land on it, instead of seeing an iceberg, they will find the label ‘Made in the USSR,’" Loeb said. articles.title: Scientists have drawn a ‘treasure map’ of where fossils of ancient sea life are still waiting to be found, after mapping 540 million years of records, and the richest untapped finds may be the youngest
articles.summary: Pirates, buckle up; there is a new treasure map in town.
articles.body: Pirates, buckle up; there is a new treasure map in town.Scientists have drawn a treasure map of where fossils of ancient sea life may still be waiting to be found. And unlike the ones that lead to buried gold, this one could help us uncover creatures that swam through Earth's oceans millions of years ago. By mapping 540 million years of fossil records, researchers have identified gaps in our understanding of prehistoric marine life and pinpointed regions that could hold clues to species yet unknown to science.Moreover, it seems like the richest opportunities for new discoveries may not lie in the distant past, where dinosaurs and other prehistoric creatures once roamed, but in comparatively younger geological periods. As it turns out, there is still plenty of history hiding beneath our feet, even if it is not quite as old as we might expect.A map of what we haven't found yetFossils are nature's time capsules. They allow scientists to reconstruct ancient ecosystems, understand how species evolved and piece together what life on Earth looked like millions of years ago. But the fossil record is far from a complete account of everything that has ever lived.For starters, fossilisation is an exceptionally rare process. When an organism dies, its remains usually decompose or are eaten by other organisms before they have a chance to become fossils. Only under particular conditions, such as rapid burial in sediment, can remains be preserved over geological time. Even then, the resulting fossils need to survive millions of years of geological changes and eventually become accessible for researchers to discover.This means that the fossils we have found so far represent only a fraction of Earth's ancient biodiversity. Some periods and geographical regions are well represented in scientific collections, while others remain poorly documented. The challenge is knowing whether a gap exists because few organisms lived there or because nobody has looked hard enough.To address this, paleontologists Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History in Germany and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna set out to map the missing pieces.Their study, published in Science Advances, examined fossil discoveries from shallow marine environments over the past 540 million years. The researchers used the Paleobiology Database, an international repository containing published fossil records, to trace where discoveries had been made throughout Earth's history.They also examined how frequently research in different regions had produced new information over time. By comparing these records with geological data from the Macrostrat database, they could identify not just places where fossils were missing from scientific records, but also locations where suitable rock formations remained accessible. In other words, the map distinguishes between places where evidence is scarce and places where there is a realistic chance of finding more.Why the oldest fossils may not be the biggest prizeOne of the more surprising findings was that the oldest geological periods may no longer be the most promising places to look for new discoveries.The researchers found that the Palaeozoic Era, which lasted from approximately 539 to 252 million years ago, and the Mesozoic Era, spanning 252 to 66 million years ago, have already been extensively studied. The former witnessed major developments in marine life, while the latter is better known as the Age of Dinosaurs.This does not mean scientists have discovered everything there is to know about these periods. Rather, the researchers suggest that additional finds from these eras are less likely to substantially expand the existing fossil record in the near future.The bigger surprise lies in the Cenozoic Era, which began around 66 million years ago and continues today. Often called the Age of Mammals, this period followed the extinction event that wiped out the non-avian dinosaurs. Mammals diversified, modern ecosystems began taking shape and marine environments continued to evolve.Despite the considerable number of fossils already recovered from this era, its shallow-water marine deposits remain comparatively underexplored. The researchers believe these sediments could hold fossils of previously undocumented species, making the Cenozoic one of the most promising frontiers for future discoveries.The Middle Miocene, approximately 15 million years ago, is one example highlighted in the researchers' maps. It represents a period with relatively few documented fossil finds but considerable potential for new discoveries.It is a reminder that younger does not necessarily mean less interesting. Sometimes, the chapters of Earth's history that appear relatively familiar are precisely the ones we have yet to read properly.Making fossil hunting more strategicOf course, finding a promising location on a map and actually digging up a fossil are two very different things. Paleontological expeditions require considerable time, funding and resources, and there is no guarantee that an excavation will produce anything new.That is where the researchers' work could prove particularly useful. Instead of repeatedly investigating locations that have already yielded extensive fossil records, scientists can use the map to prioritise regions where discoveries could add more to existing knowledge.It could also change how researchers approach natural history museums. Collections around the world contain fossils and specimens that have been gathered over decades, sometimes from regions that remain poorly represented in scientific research. Some of this material is still awaiting detailed examination. Revisiting these collections could help fill gaps in the fossil record without necessarily requiring an entirely new expedition.Neubauer believes the map could help researchers plan future excavation campaigns and focus their efforts on areas that have received comparatively little attention. The idea is to make fossil research more targeted, rather than leaving discoveries entirely to chance.There is, however, an important distinction to keep in mind. The study specifically examines animals from shallow-water marine environments. Its findings cannot automatically be extended to fossils of land-dwelling dinosaurs, prehistoric mammals or organisms from the deep sea. Those environments would require their own investigations. For now, the map offers a better understanding of where our knowledge of ancient marine life ends and where new discoveries might begin.After all, Earth's oceans have been home to an extraordinary range of life forms, many of which disappeared long before humans arrived. We have spent centuries piecing together their stories through fragments of shells, bones and other preserved remains. There may still be entire chapters waiting to be uncovered.And while this particular treasure map might not lead to a chest of gold, it could lead scientists to something considerably rarer: a species that nobody has ever seen before.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: In 2025, scientists brought pregnant San Francisco garter snakes to a zoo to protect their young; on November 10, officials revealed 62 zoo-raised snakes were released into the wild after genetic testing
articles.summary: A conservation initiative involving the San Francisco Zoo, federal wildlife officials and regional land managers has resulted in the first successful
articles.body: A conservation initiative involving the San Francisco Zoo, federal wildlife officials and regional land managers has resulted in the first successful release of zoo-raised San Francisco garter snakes into their natural habitat. According to an announcement by the San Francisco Zoo & Gardens on November 10, 2026, the programme has seen 62 young snakes return to the wild after being raised in captivity. The Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District and the US Fish and Wildlife Service have also highlighted the importance of the initiative in protecting the rare species. The project began in 2025, when biologists from the US Geological Survey collected pregnant female San Francisco garter snakes from a healthy wild population in a protected area managed by Midpen. The snakes were temporarily brought to the San Francisco Zoo, where they could give birth in a controlled environment.Once the young were born, the mothers were returned to their original habitat, while the zoo’s conservation team took responsibility for raising the newborns. The idea was to give the young snakes a better chance of surviving the early stages of life, when they are particularly vulnerable to predators and competition for food. This approach, known as head-starting, involves raising young wildlife in captivity until they reach a size at which their chances of surviving in the wild improve. It has been used in conservation programmes involving several threatened species, but this marks the first successful head-starting initiative for the San Francisco garter snake.Genetic testing determined where the snakes would goBefore the 62 young snakes were released, each underwent genetic testing to help conservationists decide where it would have the greatest impact. Around one-third were returned to the areas from which their mothers had been collected. The remaining snakes were distributed among other populations that needed additional individuals and greater genetic diversity.The strategy is intended to strengthen existing populations without placing excessive pressure on the healthy population that supplied the original breeding females. The release took place at carefully selected locations across San Mateo County, California. Authorities have deliberately withheld the exact sites to protect the animals from illegal collection, road accidents and potential exposure to disease.Why the San Francisco garter snake needs protectionThe San Francisco garter snake (Thamnophis sirtalis tetrataenia) is a distinctive reptile found naturally only on the San Francisco Peninsula, primarily in San Mateo County and parts of northern Santa Cruz County. Recognisable by its striking combination of blue-green, black and red-orange markings, it is considered one of North America’s most visually distinctive snakes.However, its restricted geographical range has made the species particularly vulnerable. It was listed as endangered under the US Endangered Species Act on March 11, 1967, making it one of the earliest species to receive federal protection under the legislation. According to the US Fish and Wildlife Service, habitat destruction, fragmentation, drought, reduced food availability and illegal collection continue to threaten its survival.The snakes also depend on healthy wetland ecosystems and prey on California red-legged frogs, another threatened species. Conservationists have therefore been working on habitat restoration alongside the breeding programme, improving wetland conditions and helping reconnect isolated wildlife populations.More than 130 baby snakes are being raised for the next releaseThe latest release is only the beginning of a longer recovery programme. The San Francisco Zoo has already welcomed more than 130 additional baby garter snakes in 2026. They are currently being raised in captivity, with another release planned for 2027.Scientists will also monitor the 62 released snakes to understand how well they adapt to their natural surroundings and whether the intervention helps strengthen existing populations. The long-term recovery target is to establish at least 10 viable, self-sustaining breeding populations, each containing a minimum of 200 snakes. Achieving this would help meet the conditions required for the species to be considered for removal from the federal endangered species list.For now, the successful return of 62 zoo-raised snakes marks an important development in a conservation effort that combines scientific research, genetic diversity and habitat protection to give one of California’s rarest reptiles a better chance of survival.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Starshield restrictions help Russia’s energy attacks on Ukraine: Zelenskyy
articles.summary: Starlink has recently denied restricting internet speeds, but Elon Musk suggested the US military could be behind it.
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that speed restrictions by Starlink’s military-grade internet service had aided a wave of deadly Russian attacks across Ukraine.

Two people were killed on Saturday in a Russian drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region.

An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity, Ukraine’s DTEK energy provider said in a Telegram statement.

Ukraine’s army said it shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

Zelenskyy posted on X that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides commonly attack each other with.

“And many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there,” he posted, citing Starlink’s sister company and reiterating accusations that it was throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations.

The president said on Saturday that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days and that Starlink reported technical problems, but Ukraine does “not believe that is the case”.

It is the second such outage in recent weeks. Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, has denied restricting internet speeds. Last month, Musk said the United States government controls Starshield.

Russia’s Defence Ministry said on Sunday that it launched attacks targeting Ukraine’s military airfields, munitions depots and other military facilities.

Authorities also said that an electrical engineer was killed and four others were injured in Russia’s Taganrog region after Ukrainian drones attacked the area on Sunday.

Six people were injured in a drone attack in Nizhnekamsk, local officials said. The city, as well as the wider Trans-Kama region of Tatarstan, reported heavy Ukrainian attacks on industrial facilities and a residential building earlier on Sunday.

US negotiators concluded visits to both countries in recent days in attempts to secure a ceasefire, despite tensions between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries.

Zelenskyy said the US floated the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for NATO membership .

Russia’s President Vladimir Putin is due to meet President Donald Trump and China’s President Xi Jinping in the Chinese city of Shenzhen this week – but Ukraine is not on the agenda. Analysts have compared the meeting to the Yalta conference of 1945, which saw the US, UK and former Soviet Union divide Germany and establish the United Nations.

However, in a statement on Sunday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, dismissed Russia’s longstanding proposal to revise Europe’s security architecture.

“Putin is throwing around ideas about reshaping the European security order. In his dreams, he sees himself in Yalta in 1945. The problem is that to put forward ideas of this magnitude, you first need to win a world war,” he said.

articles.title: ‘Almost magic’ as SpaceX craft caught mid-air: Why it matters
articles.summary: SpaceX’s Starship successfully returned to its launchpad after orbiting in space.
articles.body:
On a cloudy Saturday afternoon in the southern US state of Texas, a pair of large metallic arms stretched out and caught a giant in midair as it descended from the sky.

At 124 metres (407ft) tall, SpaceX’s Starship is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for travel to the Moon and Mars. Yet 22 hours after its latest blast off into space, it made history on Earth while returning, as it slipped smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 at Starbase city in Texas.

Aerospace engineers across the globe have lauded the first-ever capture of the upper stage of a spaceship and welcomed the achievement, which signals that mega rockets could soon be fully reusable.

Here’s why the historic capture matters:

On Saturday, after orbiting Earth 14 times for 22.5 hours, SpaceX’s Starship emerged from thick clouds over its Starbase launch site, flipped itself to a vertical position and slowly descended into the arms on the ‘Mechazilla’ launch tower.

Like massive tweezers, the arms caught the upper stage of the spacecraft in midair, while its engines were still roaring.

The spacecraft then hooked onto the tower’s mechanical arms and shut off its engines.

The roaring sound was instantly replaced by loud cheers from watchers nearby – they had just seen for the first time in history the capture of a mega rocket.

“That was the missing link, the holy grail of spaceflight,” said SpaceX mission commentator Dan Huot. “We caught a Starship and now everything changes.”

“Congratulations to an incredible team at SpaceX!!!” SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk said.

NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land astronauts on the Moon later this decade, also welcomed the achievement.

“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.

“Making more believers by the day…one step closer to [the moon],” he added.

Spacecraft returning to Earth battle gravity and a range of atmospheric factors that are nearly impossible to perfectly predict or game.

Sputnik 1, the first-ever artificial satellite sent into space, burned up while returning to Earth.

Several manned spacecraft have been destroyed while re-entering the atmosphere, killing the astronauts on board.

In April 1967, the Soviet Union’s Soyuz 1 spacecraft re-entered the atmosphere successfully, but its parachutes failed to deploy properly. Cosmonaut Vladimir Komarov died in the crash-landing near the Ural mountains. Decades later, NASA’s space shuttle Columbia disintegrated during re-entry from orbit, killing all seven astronauts on board.

In recent decades, space agencies and private firms have made major advances in safety. But many spacecraft are impossible to reuse after splashing down in the sea or on land.

Since October 2024, SpaceX has on three occasions successfully caught the boosters that propel shuttles, once they have run out of fuel and separated from the main rocket.

But until now, the main spacecraft has never been successfully caught in midair.

Soon after its return, Musk and his engineers inspected the spaceship and said that everything appeared to have worked well, including its vital heat shield.

“Ship 42 looks great!” Musk wrote on X, posting photos and videos from the launch tower.

While the capture was tricky, aerospace engineers said the upper stage catch is a big success for SpaceX.

Niharika Patel, Technical Programme Manager at Loft Orbital, a US-based space infrastructure company, told Al Jazeera that watching the catch happen was “magical.”

“Landing a rocket back on Earth is incredibly difficult and can itself be considered an engineering marvel. Now add the sheer size and weight of Starship to that equation,” she said, noting that this is also the first time the upper stage booster has been successfully caught.

“It requires incredible precision to ensure the vehicle reaches exactly the right position, withstands the extreme heat of atmospheric re-entry and executes highly controlled manoeuvres within a very tight window. And all of this happens without a pilot — it’s completely autonomous,” she added.

Why does it matter for space technology advances?

SpaceX has become dominant in the aerospace industry primarily because the company has been trying to slash the cost of space travel by launching reusable rocket technology and rapid, repeat engineering.

So far, its Falcon 9 rocket has launched 700 times since 2010, with its first stage being reusable and its second stage discarded into the sea.

With Starship, Musk has said he wants to create fully reusable flights that can also transport humans into space with minimum refurbishment.

“SpaceX has already significantly reduced the cost of getting to orbit through Falcon 9’s reusability. It’s super cheap and convenient to send satellites to low Earth orbit. Starship takes this a step further by being a much bigger craft and aiming for full reusability of both the booster and the upper stage,” Patel said.

She explained that a fully reusable vehicle can be rapidly refurbished and flown again, dramatically increasing frequency and reducing cost. So if Starship reaches this milestone, Patel said it would make access to space even more affordable and scalable, just as commercial aviation transformed travel by making aircraft reusable with quick turnaround times between flights.

“This is essential for the next era of space exploration, from deploying large satellite constellations and building space infrastructure to enabling sustained human exploration of the Moon and Mars,” Patel added.

articles.title: Archaeologists digging in Beijing have found the first Great Wall remains from the Sui dynasty in the area, a 1,400-year-old frontier outpost with weapons and pottery, plus three wooden boats about 1,800 years old
articles.summary: Archaeologists working in Beijing have uncovered the first confirmed remains of a Sui Dynasty section of the Great Wall in the Chinese capital.
articles.body: Archaeologists working in Beijing have uncovered the first confirmed remains of a Sui Dynasty section of the Great Wall in the Chinese capital. The discovery, made at the Dalinggou site in Changping district, is reshaping what researchers understand about the earliest defences around ancient Beijing. Alongside it, archaeologists have revealed three wooden boats about 1,800 years old, offering an unusually vivid picture of life, trade and transport in the region long before it became a modern metropolis.The Great Wall is often imagined as one vast, unbroken barrier. In reality, it was a shifting network of walls, watchtowers, garrisons and roads built, repaired and expanded by different states over many centuries. The new find matters because it adds a missing piece to that story: evidence that the Sui Dynasty, which ruled from 581 to 618, maintained a military presence on Beijing’s northern edge.A frontier outpost comes into viewThe excavation took place between August and October 2026, covering roughly 800 square-metres at Dalinggou in Changping. Archaeologists from the Beijing Institute of Archaeology uncovered the remains of a military outpost built against an early section of the Great Wall. Its northern wall was incorporated into the existing wall structure, while inside the enclosure were traces of buildings and retaining walls.The walls were made largely from roughly hewn stones bound and filled with loess, with an earth-and-stone core. It is a very different approach from the polished brickwork and sophisticated masonry associated with the much later Ming Dynasty wall. These older remains remind us that the Great Wall was a succession of practical frontier systems adapted to the needs and resources of their time.More than 60 artefacts were recovered from the site, including pottery, porcelain, metal objects, architectural components, everyday items and weapons. Together, they suggest that this was a working military installation, where soldiers, builders and support personnel lived, stored equipment and helped guard a strategically important northern route.Why the Sui discovery mattersBefore this excavation, the Dalinggou site had been classified as part of the Great Wall built during the Northern Qi Dynasty, which ruled from 550 to 577. The new evidence shows that the fortification was also used during the Sui Dynasty, and that parts of it remained in service centuries later, during the Jin Dynasty from 1115 to 1234.Two finds were especially important in dating the site. Archaeologists recovered a Sui-era wuzhu coin, a bronze cash coin with clear value for establishing chronology. They also found a piece of porcelain whose form and manufacturing technique closely resemble known Sui Dynasty ceramics. Individually, such objects might seem small; together, they provide strong evidence that the outpost was active during the Sui period.“This is the first discovery of Sui Dynasty Great Wall remains in the Beijing area,” said Shang Heng, an archaeologist at the Beijing Institute of Archaeology. He explained that the find is valuable for studying the age, location, direction and military defence system of the early Great Wall around Beijing. It may also help researchers trace Sui-era wall sections in neighbouring Hebei and Shanxi provinces.The discovery is particularly significant because the Sui Dynasty was short but transformative. It reunited much of China after centuries of division and laid foundations later inherited by the Tang Dynasty. Its rulers also invested heavily in securing the northern frontier, where the empire faced pressure from peoples beyond its borders. The Beijing find suggests that the Sui did not simply build new defences from nothing; it likely reused and maintained parts of the earlier Northern Qi system.A wall with a longer memoryThe site’s layered history is one of its most compelling features. A fortification first associated with the Northern Qi was later used by the Sui and still showed evidence of activity during the Jin Dynasty. That means the same landscape may have served very different rulers across more than five centuries.This challenges the popular image of the Great Wall as a static monument. Walls were not only built; they were repaired, redirected, garrisoned, abandoned and sometimes absorbed into newer defensive systems. Dalinggou offers a rare chance to see that process in one place, through its architecture and the objects left behind by the people who used it.The discovery also gives archaeologists a geographical reference point. Dalinggou lies along the same defensive line as previously identified Sui-era remains in Hebei and Shanxi. To the west, an inscription in Kelan County, Shanxi, records construction of the Great Wall in 599. To the east, another inscription from 597 was found in Luanping County, Hebei, while a Sui Dynasty beacon tower has been identified in Qianxi County.Put together, these clues suggest a broad frontier network rather than isolated local fortifications. The Beijing discovery could therefore help scholars map the route of the early wall more accurately and understand how military authority was organised across northern China.Three boats beneath BeijingThe announcement also included an equally striking discovery from Fengtai district: three ancient wooden boats, buried about seven metres underground in an old river channel. Known as Yongding River No. 1, No. 2 and No. 3, they date to roughly 1,800 years ago, during the Han and Jin dynasties.These are considered the largest and most structurally complete inland waterway vessels of their period found in northern China. Their discovery provides rare physical evidence that Beijing once had a significant inland transport network, capable of supporting official shipping and movement of goods.One boat bears the Chinese character guan, meaning official. That small mark may indicate that the vessel was built or operated under government authority. The boats also contained a sophisticated system of beams, bottom supports, vertical braces and partition boards, showing considerable skill in early Chinese shipbuilding.Archaeologists found wooden objects, woven matting and human remains associated with the vessels, along with animal bones nearby. The evidence has led researchers to a preliminary interpretation: the boats may have been damaged and gathered at a bend in the river for repair before a sudden flood buried them.What the finds revealTogether, the wall outpost and the boats paint a richer picture of early Beijing. One discovery speaks to the city’s role as a fortified frontier; the other reveals it as a place connected by rivers, transport and trade. Long before skyscrapers and highways, this was a landscape of soldiers, builders, boatmen and communities moving goods along waterways.The Great Wall remains may help explain how empires defended their northern border. The boats may reveal how people and materials moved through it. Both discoveries remind us that history is not only preserved in grand monuments. Sometimes, it survives in a coin, a shard of celadon, a timber joint, or the outline of a wall beneath a modern district.As excavation and analysis continue, Dalinggou and the Yongding River boats are likely to become important reference points for understanding Beijing’s ancient past. They show that the capital’s history extends far beyond its famous later landmarks, reaching back to an age when its fate was tied to frontier defence, river transport and the ambitions of early Chinese empires.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Beavers reintroduced to an English estate changed its stream within a year: Researchers found more land insects, higher oxygen levels and nitrate nearly disappearing downstream, with effects extending at least 1km
articles.summary: Who knew one animal could change an entire landscape?
articles.body: Who knew one animal could change an entire landscape?Beavers in an English estate did not hold meetings about biodiversity, draw up restoration blueprints or worry about water quality. They simply got to work, felling trees, building dams and creating homes around the waterways they inhabit.A recent study in England by University of Liverpool has found that reintroducing beavers to an estate in Essex transformed the surrounding stream in just a year. Researchers recorded an increase in terrestrial insects, higher oxygen levels in the water and a striking reduction in nitrate concentrations downstream. Some of these changes could be detected at least a kilometre away from the beavers' dams.The findings offer another reason to reconsider an animal that was once hunted out of Britain. They also demonstrate how restoring a species can have consequences that extend well beyond the animal itself.A landscape shaped by its inhabitantsThe animals in question are Eurasian beavers (Castor fiber), a species native to Britain that had been hunted to extinction in England around 400 years ago. Their thick fur, meat and castoreum, a substance produced by their scent glands and historically used in perfumes and medicines, made them valuable to hunters. But removing beavers also meant removing an important part of the country's natural ecosystem.Beavers are often described as ecosystem engineers. Unlike animals that simply adapt to their surroundings, they actively change them. They fell trees with their powerful front teeth, construct dams using branches, mud and vegetation, and create ponds that allow them to move through water more safely. These structures slow the movement of streams, allowing water to spread into surrounding areas and form wetlands.What might look like a rather inconvenient obstruction to a flowing stream can become an entirely new habitat for wildlife. Ponds, muddy banks, fallen trees and waterlogged vegetation offer different living conditions for insects, amphibians, birds and aquatic organisms. Even the trees felled by beavers have a second purpose, providing deadwood that supports insects and fungi.It is this ability to change the conditions around them that makes beavers particularly interesting to conservationists. Rather than simply introducing another species into an ecosystem, bringing back beavers can help restore some of the natural processes that disappeared alongside them.What happened at Spains Hall Estate?Researchers from the University of Oxford and the University of Essex, including Oliver John Sworder and Michelle Jackson, studied the effects of reintroducing beavers to enclosures at Spains Hall Estate in Essex.The team collected information about the stream's water quality, algae and invertebrate populations for a year before the beavers arrived in 2023. They then repeated their observations a year after the animals had been introduced. This before-and-after approach offered an opportunity to examine how the ecosystem changed following the reintroduction, rather than relying solely on comparisons between different streams.The findings, published alongside an openly accessible dataset on Dryad on November 3, 2026, showed that the changes were not limited to the immediate area around the dams. One of the most noticeable differences was the increase in terrestrial invertebrates, both in their abundance and species richness. In simpler terms, there were more land-dwelling invertebrates, and researchers recorded a greater variety of them.Insects and other small invertebrates are essential to the functioning of ecosystems. They pollinate plants, break down organic matter, recycle nutrients and provide food for birds, fish, amphibians and other animals. An increase in their numbers can therefore have consequences that travel up the food chain.The researchers also examined freshwater invertebrates, but the findings here were more complicated. There was no statistically significant increase in overall freshwater invertebrate richness, abundance or biomass. However, certain indicator groups were affected, and the composition of feeding groups within the stream changed. In other words, the beavers did not simply make every category of aquatic insect more plentiful. They altered the conditions in which different organisms lived and fed.The surprising effect on water qualityPerhaps the most striking finding concerned the water itself. Researchers recorded an increase in dissolved oxygen throughout the stream following the beavers' arrival. Dissolved oxygen is exactly what it sounds like: oxygen present in water, which aquatic organisms rely on to survive. Fish, insect larvae and other freshwater animals need sufficient oxygen to carry out essential biological processes. When oxygen levels fall too low, aquatic ecosystems can become difficult places to survive.The researchers also examined nitrate concentrations, which offered another interesting result. Nitrate is a naturally occurring form of nitrogen, but excessive amounts entering waterways can become a serious environmental problem. Agricultural fertilisers, animal waste and other sources can introduce additional nitrogen into streams and rivers. When concentrations become too high, they can encourage excessive algae growth. As this algae dies and decomposes, microorganisms consume oxygen in the process, potentially leaving less available for other aquatic life.Here, the researchers noticed something rather unexpected. Nitrate concentrations increased in the water around the beaver dams, but downstream, the nitrate was almost completely filtered out following the reintroduction.Beaver dams can slow water movement, allowing sediment and organic material to settle rather than being carried further downstream. The wetlands they create can also encourage biological processes through which nitrogen is absorbed by vegetation or converted into nitrogen gas by microorganisms. These processes can help remove excess nitrogen from waterways.Although the study does not establish that one particular mechanism was responsible for the changes, the results suggest that beaver activity can influence how nutrients move through an ecosystem.Even more interestingly, the effects were not confined to the immediate surroundings of the dams. Researchers found that the changes extended at least a kilometre downstream. This suggests that the ecological benefits of beaver activity can travel considerably further than the structures the animals build.A little more room for natureThe findings arrive at an interesting time for conservation in Britain. After centuries of absence, beavers are gradually returning to English waterways through managed reintroduction programmes and the expansion of existing populations.In February 2025, the British government announced that wild releases of beavers in England would be permitted under licences issued by Natural England. The decision marked an important step towards restoring a species that once played a natural role in shaping the country's rivers and wetlands.However, bringing back beavers is not without its complications. Their dams can cause localised flooding, affect agricultural land and change the availability of habitats for certain species. Watercourses do not exist in isolation from people, and the interests of farmers, landowners and nearby communities must be considered when deciding where reintroductions should take place. The benefits also depend on the characteristics of individual landscapes, so what works in one location may not necessarily work in another.There is also an important distinction to make about the latest research. The observations were collected over a relatively short period of one year, at a managed estate. They offer encouraging evidence of how quickly ecological changes can begin, but longer-term monitoring will be needed to understand whether these improvements persist and how they develop over time.Still, the study makes a compelling case for looking at conservation differently. Protecting an ecosystem does not always mean intervening in every little detail. Sometimes, it means bringing back the species that already know how to look after it.Beavers build dams because they need deeper water and safer places to live. They fell trees because they need food and building materials. Yet, in meeting their own needs, they create habitats for countless other organisms, alter the movement of water and influence the nutrients flowing through it.A year after their arrival, the stream at Spains Hall Estate was already showing signs of these changes. There were more land-dwelling invertebrates, higher oxygen levels and considerably less nitrate downstream.Perhaps the most encouraging part is that the beavers were not introduced to perform any of these individual tasks. They were simply given a place to live and allowed to do what comes naturally. Sometimes, nature's most effective restoration workers are already there.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Trump moves to build his space legacy with NASA’s help
articles.summary: President Trump is about to do JFK one better.
articles.body:
Lost in the glare of the recent midterms and their startling results, President Trump released a proclamation entitled The American Declaration of Freedom in Space . The document states that American policy will be to open up the solar system “forging an interplanetary civilization founded on the enduring and inalienable rights of freedom and individual liberty.”

Summoning the legacy of the Apollo moon landings and the ongoing Artemis program, Trump’s proclamation set an ultimate goal for America’s space effort that goes beyond just returning to the moon and going on to Mars.

It states that “the solar system and all of outer space beyond Earth are the province of all humans and are open to exploration, development, use, and the establishment of a permanent presence by American citizens consistent with United States law and the international obligations of the United States.”

As noted, the proclamation does not set aside the Outer Space Treaty by claiming the solar system for the U.S. as sovereign territory. But it is firm in the principle that the U.S. will lead the winning of the high frontier of space.

A few short years ago, Trump’s proclamation and the vision contained within it would have seemed to be more a scenario of a science fiction story than government policy. Now, the document has been barely remarked on, even by critics. The wide acceptance of the Artemis program and the rise of the commercial space sector, as exemplified by SpaceX and Blue Origin, have made dreams of an interplanetary civilization into a likely future.

Three days after the midterms, President Trump traveled to the Kennedy Space Center in Florida to deliver remarks at Max Power , a technology exhibition and air show. Some of his speech covered the midterms and more Earthly issues. But the heart of what the president had to say celebrated the space program, as well as technological advances such as nuclear power and the Human Genome Project. He noted the upcoming Artemis IV moon landing, with missions scheduled to begin in 2028, the final year of his current and last term in office.

The very next day, NASA announced contracts issued under the next phase of the Commercial Lunar Payload Services program.

“The investments will advance commercial robotic deliveries, a nuclear-powered rover named PROMISE, launch and orbital transfer services, and surface infrastructure as the agency works with American industry to establish a sustained presence on the Moon’s South Pole.”

No matter what happens, Donald Trump will not be president of the United States after Jan. 20, 2029. After the thumping that the Republicans received in the recent midterms, Trump has two things to do. He has to hold the line against emboldened congressional Democrats, and he has to build a lasting legacy.

The first task should be straightforward. Like President Obama after his midterm defeat in 2014, Trump has a veto pen and a phone. He will have to fend off attacks on Elon Musk, the entrepreneur crucial to the spread of human civilization across the solar system.

For the second task, Trump should look to the example of President Reagan after the 1986 midterm elections. Reagan was the subject of endless investigations and threats of impeachment surrounding the Iran-Contra scandal, just as Trump is likely to be because of a multitude of real and perceived sins.

Despite all that, Reagan left office with a 63 percent approval rating . Then, when the Berlin Wall fell, followed by the Soviet Union, he became a world historic figure, mentioned in the same breath as Washington and Lincoln. Incidentally, Reagan’s legacy also includes the orbiting laboratory that eventually became known as the International Space Station.

If all goes as planned, in the midst of the tiresome veto fights and endless investigations, in 2028, American astronauts will walk on the moon. America and the world will stop and watch in wonder at the sight, not seen since Richard Nixon was in office.

No matter what one feels about Trump, hate him or love him, the unalterable fact will be that he set that next moonwalk in motion. The Artemis program has survived changes of administrations and congresses. It is one thing that most Americans, on both sides of the political divide, agree is glorious and good.

Think of President John F. Kennedy. Two things are remembered of him. He was assassinated and he threw down the gauntlet for the race to the moon.

President Trump is about to do Kennedy one better. The Apollo program ended. The Artemis program and what will follow will never end. Not a bad legacy.

Mark R. Whittington, who writes frequently about space policy, has published a political study of space exploration entitled “ Why is It So Hard to Go Back to the Moon? ” as well as “ The Moon, Mars and Beyond ” and, most recently, “ Why is America Going Back to the Moon? ” He blogs at Curmudgeons Corner.

articles.title: In October, rescuers found hundreds of chinchillas confined in filthy cages at an Ohio breeder; by November 3, Humane World for Animals had removed 951, and federal action forced the facility to close
articles.summary: A breeding facility in Jenera, Ohio, became the centre of a federal animal welfare case after inspectors discovered hundreds of chinchillas living in
articles.body: A breeding facility in Jenera, Ohio, became the centre of a federal animal welfare case after inspectors discovered hundreds of chinchillas living in severely neglected conditions. Rows of cramped cages, untreated medical conditions and animals kept in a building that had allegedly been hidden from inspectors for years prompted legal action against the breeder. Following a request from the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), Humane World for Animals stepped in to help remove the animals.The organisation's Animal Rescue Team completed the rescue of 951 chinchillas in two operations. Rescuers first entered the facility on October 13 and removed 642 animals over two days. On November 3, the team returned to collect another 309 chinchillas after federal authorities secured the surrender of the remaining animals.The rescue followed years of inspections and alleged violations of the federal Animal Welfare Act at R&R Chinchilla Inc. Veterinary examinations after the animals reached safety revealed the extent of their suffering, with many showing signs of chronic health problems. The breeding facility's owner has since agreed to surrender the animals and permanently stop activities regulated under the Animal Welfare Act.What did inspectors discover inside the Ohio chinchilla breeding facility?The federal investigation began after the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) referred the case to the Justice Department, warning that animals at the facility faced serious danger. In August 2026, the DOJ filed a complaint against R&R Chinchilla Inc. and its president, James F. Ritterspach, alleging repeated failures to meet the Animal Welfare Act's standards for animal care.According to the complaint, the USDA conducted 18 inspections of the facility between September 2022 and August 2026. Inspectors identified multiple violations during nearly every inspection, recording 59 violations over four years. Seventeen of these were classified as critical or direct because they had serious adverse effects on the animals' health and well-being.One of the most troubling discoveries came on August 5, when USDA inspectors gained access to a second building that had allegedly remained hidden from inspection for years. The breeder had reportedly told inspectors that the facility housed between 300 and 450 chinchillas. However, officials alleged that approximately 800 additional animals lived in the undisclosed structure.Inspectors described the building as being in worse condition than any facility they had previously examined. Hundreds of enclosures had floors covered in faecal matter, while ammonia levels became so high that inspectors started coughing and had to leave. They also found open packets of rat poison near the chinchilla enclosures and multiple dead animals inside the building.Some chinchillas had eyes so swollen and filled with discharge that they could not open them. Another animal had a metal collar tightly embedded in the neck. Inspectors also documented an incident in which Ritterspach allegedly held a badly matted chinchilla by the tail and pulled a large section of tangled fur from her body, leaving an exposed patch of skin.How did Humane World for Animals rescue the 951 chinchillas?The DOJ requested assistance from Humane World for Animals after federal authorities began legal proceedings against the breeder. The organisation's Animal Rescue Team entered the facility on October 13, 2026, and spent two days removing 642 chinchillas.The second operation took place on November 3, after the federal government secured an agreement for the surrender of the remaining animals. Rescuers returned to Jenera and removed another 309 chinchillas, bringing the total number relocated by the organisation to 951.The rescue formed part of a wider legal effort to remove the animals from the breeding operation. On August 20, the DOJ had filed a motion seeking a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction. The court granted the temporary restraining order on August 21 and subsequently approved a modified order requiring the surrender of approximately 800 chinchillas.On November 2, the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Ohio endorsed a consent decree under which Ritterspach agreed to surrender the remaining animals and permanently stop activities regulated under the Animal Welfare Act. The USDA also permanently revoked his federal animal welfare licence, bringing the breeding operation to an end.What kind of homes will the rescued chinchillas need?Humane World for Animals is working with its network of shelters and rescue partners to arrange suitable placements for the 951 chinchillas. However, finding homes for so many animals requires careful planning because chinchillas have specialised needs and can live for up to 20 years in captivity.Native to the Andes Mountains of South America, chinchillas are social animals that naturally live in groups. They need opportunities to explore, exercise, hide and interact with other chinchillas. They also require regular dust baths to maintain their dense coats.Unlike dogs and cats, which humans have selectively bred for companionship over thousands of years, chinchillas entered the pet trade relatively recently, during the early 20th century. They remain wild animals with natural behaviours that owners must accommodate. Humane World for Animals is therefore looking for adopters who understand the long-term commitment involved and can provide appropriate living conditions, companionship and veterinary care. The Ohio case has also drawn attention to the wider problems associated with the commercial trade in wild animals. Chinchillas face threats in their natural habitats from hunting for fur, habitat loss, poaching and the pet trade. Captive breeding operations can create further welfare concerns when animals live in overcrowded or poorly maintained conditions.The removal of 951 chinchillas from R&R Chinchilla Inc. has given these animals an opportunity to recover from years of alleged neglect. But their rescue is only the beginning. The next challenge is ensuring that they receive the care, space and companionship they need for the rest of their lives.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: After tracking more than 440 female Asian elephants in Sri Lanka for 12 years, US researchers found that population losses were followed by a sudden breakdown in social networks, leaving smaller and more isolated groups
articles.summary: Elephants are known for their strong family bonds and complex social relationships, but declining populations may be putting these connections at risk.
articles.body: Elephants are known for their strong family bonds and complex social relationships, but declining populations may be putting these connections at risk. A 12-year study in Sri Lanka has found that the gradual loss of individual elephants can eventually trigger a sudden breakdown in their social networks, leaving surviving animals in smaller and more isolated communities.The research, led by scientists at the University of California San Diego (UC San Diego) and published in the journal Science on November 12, 2026, examined more than 440 wild female Asian elephants at Udawalawe National Park in Sri Lanka. The findings, reported by UC San Diego in a November 12 research announcement by Mario Aguilera, suggest that the population appears to have crossed a social tipping point after years of demographic changes, making its once closely connected communities increasingly fragmented.Population losses preceded social changesThe researchers analysed the social relationships of 443 female Asian elephants over 12 years, examining how their associations and community structures changed as individual animals disappeared from the population. Their findings showed that gradual demographic turnover eventually preceded a sudden change in the elephants' social networks. The population experienced a combination of likely deaths, permanent departures from the area and fewer new individuals joining the community.As these losses accumulated, the elephants shifted from larger, densely connected social communities to smaller groups with fewer connections between them. The research was led by postdoctoral researcher Anastasia Madsen, working with Associate Professor Shermin de Silva and other researchers. Madsen explained that the population was losing individuals at increasing rates without enough new elephants arriving to replace them.The researchers also found that the changes went beyond simply having fewer elephants. The surviving animals were altering their relationships with one another, further weakening the overall structure of their social networks.Why social connections matter to elephantsAsian elephants are highly social animals that depend on relationships with other members of their communities for several aspects of their lives. According to the UC San Diego research announcement, these connections help elephants find food, obtain information and raise their young. Established relationships also allow individuals to benefit from the knowledge and experience of other elephants. When population numbers decline, the loss of individual animals can therefore affect much more than the size of a herd. It can also remove important social connections that help communities function.Shermin de Silva, an associate professor at UC San Diego, explained that maintaining strong social networks requires animals to share space and build relationships throughout their lives. For communities to remain resilient, lost relationships must be replaced over time. The researchers warned that fewer opportunities to establish new connections could leave surviving elephants increasingly isolated.Human activities may worsen the problemThe study's findings come against a wider backdrop of threats facing Asian elephants. Poaching and conflicts with humans have already contributed to elephant deaths in many populations. The researchers also identified potential pressures affecting the Udawalawe National Park population, including disruptions to habitat connectivity and reduced food availability as ecological conditions change across the park and its surroundings.Udawalawe National Park covers approximately 119 square miles, and changes in the surrounding landscape can affect how elephants move between areas and maintain contact with other groups. However, the study does not attribute every disappearance to a single cause. Its findings focus on how accumulated population losses and demographic turnover were associated with changes in social organisation.Researchers warn of a difficult-to-reverse tipping pointOne of the most important findings is that social fragmentation may not be easily reversed once a population crosses a critical threshold. Madsen warned that gradual changes can build up over time before producing a sudden shift in an animal community's structure. Once that tipping point is crossed, returning to the previous social organisation can become much harder. The researchers said the findings highlight why conservation efforts should consider not only how many animals remain in a population but also how they interact with one another.The study, titled Increased demographic turnover and isolation precede social fragmentation in Asian elephants, provides evidence that monitoring social relationships could help identify problems in wildlife populations before their consequences become more difficult to address. It also highlights the importance of protecting habitats and maintaining conditions that allow elephants to move, form relationships and sustain their communities.Your child uses AI every day.
