articles.title: Vulcan rocket fails, destroying 40 Amazon Leo satellites
articles.summary: ULA said an ‘anomaly’ led to its Vulcan vehicle failing to deliver its payload of Amazon Leo satellites to orbit.
articles.body: United Launch Alliance (ULA) suffered what is reportedly its first mission failure in its 20-year history, failing to deliver 40 Amazon Leo satellites to orbit. Leo is Amazon’s competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink, but it has struggled to get off the ground so far, putting only a small portion of the necessary satellites to challenge Starlink into orbit. Today’s launch was supposed to be the first of 38 flights Amazon purchased from ULA. In a statement posted on X, ULA said, “Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” [Media: The company said it was currently unclear what caused the failure, but pledged transparency as it continues its investigation. Amazon projected confidence in its launch partner despite the failure, posting on X that, “ There is risk with any launch, and that’s especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01. ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they’ll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan.”

articles.title: From Chandrayaan-3 to Space Vision 2047: Leadership that turns aspiration into national capability
articles.summary: India's journey to Moon, Space Vision for Amrit Kaal and the opening of the space sector demonstrate how visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra
articles.body: India's journey to Moon, Space Vision for Amrit Kaal and the opening of the space sector demonstrate how visionary leadership of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and govt, institutional resilience and collective ownership can transform ambitious national goals into extraordinary achievements.India's successful landing of Chandrayaan-3 on Moon on Aug 23, 2023, was much more than a technological milestone. It represented the coming together of national vision, political leadership, institutional commitment, scientific determination and the collective efforts of thousands of people. It demonstrated an important principle of nation-building: extraordinary achievements become possible when individual aspirations are transformed into a shared national mission.Having been closely associated with India's space programme, I see Chandrayaan-3 not as an isolated success, but as the outcome of decades of institution-building, technological development and perseverance. It offers valuable lessons on leadership, particularly in large national programmes.The Indian space programme began in the early 1960s with very modest resources. The establishment of INCOSPAR in 1962, ISRO in 1969 and department of space in 1972 laid the foundations for national space capability. From sounding rockets at Thumba to sophisticated launch vehicles, satellites and planetary missions, India built technological capabilities through sustained commitment. Such a journey requires more than scientific excellence. It requires leadership that establishes a long-term vision and sustains institutional confidence.One significant leadership moment was the articulation of India's Space Vision 2047, approved by the minister as an aspirational goal for Amrit Kaal. It provided a long-term framework encompassing human spaceflight, Bharatiya Antariksh Station, advanced heavy-lift and reusable launch vehicles, sustained human presence in space and deeper lunar exploration, including an Indian landing on Moon. Equally important was financial approval for initial programmes.Another leadership decision was opening the Indian space sector to private participation, followed by Indian Space Policy 2023. With ISRO established as a successful national agency, young entrepreneurs and innovators wanted to enter the domain. Recognising that the future scale and economic impact of space activities required capabilities beyond a govt organisation, the reforms created opportunities for private enterprises. The objective was not to diminish ISRO's role, but to expand collective capacity by enabling industry, start-ups and research institutions to contribute. Around 440 registered space-technology start-ups by August 2026 reflect this enthusiasm.Chandrayaan-2 provides another important leadership lesson. Its landing attempt in Sept 2019 didn't achieve the intended soft landing. Yet, the response was not to abandon the ambition. The mission was examined, shortcomings analysed and improvements incorporated into Chandrayaan-3, with attention to landing-system robustness and uncertainties.Chandrayaan-3 showed that failure, approached with openness and scientific discipline, becomes a source of institutional learning.PM Modi's participation on Chandrayaan-3's landing day and interaction with the mission team gave the achievement wider public significance. Recognition of scientists and engineers, including women scientists and project leaders, reinforced that national achievements are built through collective effort at every institutional level.Behind Chandrayaan-3 was an enormous organisational effort. This is where institutional leadership becomes critical. The role of a leader is not to provide every technical answer, but to create an environment in which the right questions are asked, technical disagreements are encouraged, decisions are based on evidence and competent teams are empowered to take responsibility. Problems must be reported without fear, and accountability must exist at every level. Excessive centralisation can delay decisions, while decentralisation without accountability can fragment an effort. Successful mission leadership requires a balance between the two.Operational leadership matters equally. Engineers, technicians, scientists, quality-assurance personnel, industrial partners and ground teams determine mission reliability. Younger professionals bring new ideas; experienced colleagues contribute institutional knowledge. Integrating these strengths is essential.The lesson extends beyond space. Large national programmes need clear objectives, continuity, coordination, ownership and a culture of learning. Gaganyaan, Bharatiya Antariksh Station, advanced launch vehicles and future lunar missions require capabilities of greater scale and partnerships among govt, public institutions, industry, universities and start-ups.From Thumba to Chandrayaan-3, India's journey illustrates what sustained commitment and decisive leadership can achieve. Progress depends not only on technology but also on the institutions we build, the people we empower and the leadership that gives direction to their collective efforts.(The writer, a former Isro chairman, is chancellor of Chanakya University)Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Scientists discover star system sending strange radio signals every eight minutes from deep space
articles.summary: A group of researchers has discovered a mysterious star system more than 5,000 light-years away that emits radio signals every eight minutes.
articles.body:
Researchers discovered a mysterious star system that emits radio signals every eight minutes.

One of the stars is a white dwarf. The other is a G-type star which is similar to the Sun.

These star systems belong to a group known as long-period transients, which produce radio signals that turn on and off.

A group of researchers has discovered a mysterious star system more than 5,000 light-years away that emits radio signals every eight minutes.

Scientists at Curtin University's node of the International Centre for Radio Astronomy Research (ICRAR) in Perth, Australia , have linked the rare radio pulses to an unusual star system known as GPM J071507−114153.

The system consists of two stars orbiting each other: a dead star that spins every eight minutes and another star similar to our own Sun .

One of the stars is a white dwarf, the dense core left behind when a star dies. The other is a G-type star, a classification that includes our own Sun.

"We detected this system in a large survey using the MWA (Murchison Widefield Array) to scan the entire Milky Way visible from Australia. We then used the MeerKAT radio telescope in South Africa to determine its precise position," Associate Professor Natasha Hurley-Walker, a co-author of the paper, said.

The team analyzed more than 100 hours of radio data to better understand the movement of the white dwarf.

"This is the first time the pulses are clear enough to see the white dwarf moving in its orbit around its companion, so we know that the pulsations are coming from a region close to the white dwarf, or possibly even from the white dwarf itself," lead author and Square Kilometre Array Observatory commissioning scientist Dr. Sam McSweeney said.

Typically, these types of radio signals have been detected coming from systems containing smaller, cooler stars known as red dwarfs.

However, this newly discovered system is different because it includes a star similar to our own Sun, making it a rare find.

"It's amazing that by using radio wavelengths we can detect the storms on a star over 5000 light-years away," Associate Professor Hurley-Walker said.

These star systems belong to a group known as long-period transients (LPTs), which produce radio signals that turn on and off at intervals ranging from a few minutes to several hours.

Since the first LPT system was discovered in 2021, astronomers have identified only about a dozen others.

While several previously discovered systems also contain a white dwarf paired with another star, scientists have not been able to determine which star is responsible for producing the unusual radio signals.

"If we are already making such discoveries with precursor telescopes, just imagine how many more star systems we will be able to find," Associate Professor Hurley-Walker said.

articles.title: Voyager 1, da Nasa, vai atingir marco histórico de um dia-luz | G1
articles.standfirst: Lançada em 1977, a Voyager 1 está prestes a alcançar a distância de 26 bilhões de quilômetros da Terra, equivalente ao percurso da luz em 24 horas. Será a primeira sonda a atingir essa marca.
articles.summary: Lançada em 1977, sonda será o primeiro objeto construído pelo ser humano a alcançar cerca de 26 bilhões de quilômetros da Terra, distância que a luz percorre em 24 horas.
articles.body:
Ilustração mostra sonda Voyager, da Nasa, viajando pelo espaço interestelar. — Foto: NASA/JPL-Caltech/Reuters

A Voyager 1, da Nasa, já viajou mais longe do que qualquer outra sonda espacial partindo da Terra desde seu lançamento, em 1977.

A sonda, que saiu do nosso sistema solar há anos e está viajando pelo espaço interestelar, está agora prestes a atingir um marco notável — transpor um dia-luz, a distância que a luz percorre em 24 horas.

Um dia-luz equivale a cerca de 26 bilhões de quilômetros. A agência espacial dos EUA informou que a Voyager 1, voando a quase 61.000 km/h pelo vácuo virtual do espaço, alcançará essa distância da Terra na quarta-feira, às 7h16 (horário de Brasília).

A sonda robótica tem a distinção de ser o objeto feito pelo homem mais distante.

“Vejo isso como um marco da engenharia, que marca a incrível longevidade da Voyager 1 — e também como uma conquista da engenharia poder se comunicar com a Voyager 1 a essa distância”, disse o astrofísico Alan Cummings, pesquisador sênior do Laboratório de Radiação Espacial da Caltech, que atua como cientista do programa Voyager desde 1973.

Um ano-luz pode ser um conceito mais familiar para muitas pessoas, uma unidade de medida usada para distâncias cósmicas vastas.

É a distância que uma partícula de luz, chamada fóton, percorre em um ano — cerca de 9,5 trilhões de quilômetros .

Por exemplo, as estrelas mais próximas além do nosso sistema solar são as três que compõem o sistema Alfa Centauri, a cerca de 4,24 anos-luz de distância.

A Voyager 1 e sua nave gêmea, a Voyager 2, foram lançadas há 49 anos, explorando planetas no sistema solar exterior antes de seguirem adiante.

A Voyager 1 foi lançada ao espaço em 5 de setembro de 1977, a bordo de um foguete Titan IIIE-Centaur, partindo de Cabo Canaveral, na Flórida, 16 dias após o lançamento da Voyager 2, mas ultrapassou sua gêmea em poucos meses.

“A Voyager 1 trouxe uma grande quantidade de novas informações sobre Júpiter e Saturno, e suas luas”, disse Cummings.

Ela descobriu um anel fino ao redor de Júpiter e duas luas jovianas até então não detectadas. Em seguida, identificou cinco novas luas ao redor de Saturno, bem como um anel chamado de anel G.

“A Voyager 2 seguiu uma trajetória diferente pelo sistema solar após o lançamento em 1977, a fim de visitar Urano e Netuno. A Voyager 2 está a caminho de ficar a um dia-luz da Terra em mais nove anos, em novembro de 2035”, disse Cummings.

articles.title: Scientists discovered a deep-sea worm living inside a glass sponge 1,000 metres below the Pacific; it uses the sponge as a hiding place to ambush other animals
articles.summary: A deep-sea worm living inside a glass sponge more than 1,000 metres beneath the Pacific Ocean has been identified as a new species, revealing an unique
articles.body: A deep-sea worm living inside a glass sponge more than 1,000 metres beneath the Pacific Ocean has been identified as a new species, revealing an unique relationship between two marine animals. The worm uses the sponge as a sheltered hiding place, waiting for other creatures to come within reach before feeding. Researchers described the discovery in a 2025 study titled 'Ambusher in sponge: a new species of Eunice (Annelida, Eunicidae) commensal within deep-sea Farreidae (Porifera, Hexactinellida) on northwest Pacific seamounts.' The findings also suggest that the arrangement could benefit both animals.Deep-sea worm hiding inside a glass sponge uses an unusual hunting strategyThe newly described species, named Eunice siphoninsidiator, lives in the central cavity of deep-sea glass sponges belonging to the Farreidae family. According to the ZooKeys study, the worm was discovered on seamounts in the north-west Pacific, where researchers examined specimens collected during deep-sea expeditions.Instead of living freely on the sea floor, the worm lives inside the sponge. This puts it in a safe spot but allows it to remain close to potential prey as it moves around the surrounding marine environment.The researchers identified the animal as a member of the Eunicidae family, a group of marine worms. Its particular association with glass sponges, however, makes it distinct from many other members of the group.A sheltered position helps the worm wait for preyThe worm's unique home appears to play an important role in how it feeds. Researchers examined fragments recovered from its digestive tract and found evidence of a carnivorous diet.The ZooKeys paper reports that the gut contained fragments of stalked barnacles and brittle stars. Although the researchers could not identify the remains to the species level, the material provided clues about what the worm consumes.Our results indicate that Eunice siphoninsidiator employs a sit-and-wait hunting strategy. It doesn’t appear to actively hunt across the seabed for food, but instead to stay hidden inside the sponge, and ambushes animals that come close enough to be captured. This behaviour explains the significance of the species' scientific name, which reflects its ambush-oriented lifestyle.The sponge may benefit from its unusual residentThe relationship between the worm and its host is not necessarily one-sided. "The animal living inside the sponge's central cavity might also benefit the sponge," the researchers suggest.The worm could help remove organisms growing on the surface of the sponge, the study says. These are called epibionts , and they can attach to other living organisms in the sea .The worm may help keep its host relatively clean by feeding on animals associated with the sponge. The researchers therefore consider the association to be potentially mutualistic, where both organisms could gain from their association.The study also makes an important observation. The worm was always within the glass sponges the researchers examined. This repeated association suggests the animal is closely adapted to the sponge habitat and not just using it by chance.Researchers identified the worm through physical and genetic evidenceThe researchers also studied its physical features and genetic material to see if it was a new species not previously described.The study describes Eunice siphoninsidiator as very similar to the Atlantic Ocean species Eunice norvegica. Both its physical appearance and molecular characteristics showed similarities.But the researchers identified differences that helped distinguish the newly described worm. These included the relative length of its palps, the structures around its head, the positions where certain hooks begin along its body and the shape of its bristles.Genetic analysis provided further evidence. The researchers compared a section of the animals' DNA known as the cytochrome c oxidase subunit I gene, or COI, and found a genetic distance of 13% between the new species and Eunice norvegica. This difference supported the researchers' conclusion that the sponge-dwelling worm should be recognised as a separate species.Deep-sea sponges provide habitats for other animalsThe discovery also points to the role of deep-sea sponges in supporting marine life. Glass sponges make intricate structures that can offer shelter and habitat to other organisms in places where good homes may be scarce.In the study, the researchers explain that deep-sea sponges attract a variety of associated animals including species that live with or inside them. Eunice siphoninsidiator is one example of how such relationships can develop in the deep ocean.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? Find out in the TOI AI Masterclass.

articles.title: Scientists identified a new deepwater fish in the South China Sea after noticing unusual facial stripes; its markings reminded them of a character from ‘Princess Mononoke’
articles.summary: Scientists have identified a new deepwater fish in the South China Sea after discovering unusual stripes on its cheeks that reminded them of San, the
articles.body: Scientists have identified a new deepwater fish in the South China Sea after discovering unusual stripes on its cheeks that reminded them of San, the warrior princess from Studio Ghibli's 1997 animated film Princess Mononoke. Named Branchiostegus sanae, the newly identified species was confirmed through genetic analysis by a team of Chinese researchers. Its distinctive orange and white facial markings inspired the scientific name, which pays tribute to the character known for her red war paint and efforts to protect the forest. The discovery adds another species to the relatively small group of deepwater tilefish.Unusual facial stripes reveal a new deepwater fish speciesThe newly identified fish belongs to the deepwater tilefish family Branchiostegidae. Its most noticeable feature is a pattern of orange and white stripes beneath its eye, which distinguishes it from other members of its group. Researchers noticed these unusual cheek markings and named the species Branchiostegus sanae in tribute to the fictional warrior princess.The identification was confirmed through genetic analysis conducted by researchers from the South China Sea Institute of Oceanology, the Chinese Academy of Sciences, Zhejiang University and Ocean University of China. Their work established that the specimen represented a species not previously described by science. The findings added another species to the Branchiostegus genus, which forms part of the wider deepwater tilefish family.‘Princess Mononoke’ character behind the fish's nameThe species name sanae was inspired by San, the warrior princess from Princess Mononoke, the 1997 animated film directed by Hayao Miyazaki. San is a young woman who is raised by wolves after being abandoned by her human parents. Recognisable by the red markings on her face, she considers herself part of the forest and fights to defend it.Lead author Haochen Huang explained the reasoning behind the name, drawing a connection between the film's environmental themes and the researchers' choice. According to the BBC, Huang said: "The film delves into the complex relationship between humans and nature, promoting a message of harmonious coexistence between the two: something we hope to echo through this naming." The naming therefore pays tribute to the character while reflecting the film's message about the relationship between people and the natural world.What makes deepwater tilefish different from other marine speciesDeepwater tilefish belong to the family Branchiostegidae and are found in marine environments at considerable depths. Some species in this group have been recorded as deep as 600 metres below the ocean surface. They are also commonly found in seafood markets across East and Southeast Asia.Despite their presence in regional seafood markets, the diversity of the group remains limited. At the time of the report, scientists had described 31 species in the Branchiostegidae family, including 19 species belonging to the Branchiostegus genus. The identification of Branchiostegus sanae adds to the documented diversity of this group.Why the new deepwater fish discovery is considered rareThe identification of the new fish is particularly significant because relatively few new species have been recorded within the genus in recent decades. According to the BBC, only three new species of Branchiostegus had been identified in the preceding 34 years.Haochen Huang described the discovery as an uncommon finding, saying: "Finding a new species in this group is a rare and fortunate event, especially one as distinctive as Branchiostegus sanae,". Following its identification, specimens of the fish were preserved in marine biological collections. These preserved specimens will allow scientists to examine the species further and support future research into deepwater tilefish.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.body: Amazon lost 40 satellites intended for its Leo satellite internet network after a Vulcan rocket operated by United Launch Alliance (ULA), a joint venture between Boeing and Lockheed Martin, failed shortly after liftoff from Florida on November 15. The failure marks the first mission loss for ULA and is a setback for Amazon as it works to expand its satellite internet constellation and compete with SpaceX’s Starlink. The rocket suffered an anomaly around 10 minutes into the flight, preventing it from delivering Amazon’s satellites into orbit. While the cause of the failure was not immediately clear, the incident is expected to trigger a technical investigation that could keep Vulcan grounded for months.Amazon responds to satellite lossAmazon said that risks are associated with every rocket launch, particularly during early missions. The company also expressed confidence in ULA’s ability to investigate the failure."There is risk with any launch, and that's especially true for inaugural missions like LV-01," Amazon said in a statement, referring to the name of Sunday's mission. "ULA has been a trusted partner for Amazon, and we believe they'll learn from this mission and deliver on their long-term plans for Vulcan."ULA confirms Vulcan rocket failureThe Vulcan rocket lifted off from Space Launch Complex 41 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Around 10 minutes into the flight, the rocket encountered an anomaly, according to ULA.“Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 ​suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit,” ULA said in a statement.The company added that it was too early to determine what caused the failure.“Every flight generates data, and ​every flight teaches us something. Since the anomaly just occurred, we don't have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today,” ULA ⁠said.The mission was Vulcan’s fifth flight since its debut in 2024 and its first launch in nine months. The rocket had remained grounded following technical investigations into its solid rocket side boosters and core BE-4 engines.The loss of the 40 satellites adds to the challenges Amazon has faced in deploying its Leo internet constellation. articles.body: The Australian Reptile Park has welcomed the first king cobras to hatch in Australia in 16 years. According to the Park, the breeding pair were introduced in September 2025, and the female, Medusa, built a nest and laid her eggs in November. Park Manager Billy Collett decided to incubate the eggs artificially to give them the best chance of survival, and three highly venomous hatchlings emerged, each under 30 centimetres long. The Park says this is the third successful king cobra breeding event recorded in Australia, all at the Park. The last hatching was in 2010. articles.standfirst: Los investigadores localizan terrenos que podrían esconder restos de este tipo aún por descubrir
articles.summary: Los investigadores localizan terrenos que podrían esconder restos de este tipo aún por descubrir
articles.body: Para encontrar fósiles de animales que vivieron en mares poco profundos, dos paleontólogos han puesto el foco en terrenos que hoy se pueden recorrer a pie. Thomas A. Neubauer, de las Colecciones Estatales de Ciencias Naturales de Baviera, y Mathias Harzhauser, del Museo de Historia Natural de Viena, han elaborado un mapa mundial que abarca 540 millones de años y señala dónde merece la pena excavar. El estudio, publicado en Science Advances, parte de una pregunta: si en una región apenas se han encontrado fósiles, ¿significa que allí vivían pocos animales? Una concha puede deshacerse antes de quedar enterrada, pero también es posible que se conserve en una capa de roca que los investigadores apenas han explorado. Los autores reconstruyeron la extensión de los antiguos mares y situaron sobre esos mapas los hallazgos documentados. Después consultaron la cartografía geológica actual para localizar terrenos donde coinciden dos pistas, se conocen pocos fósiles y todavía quedan rocas de la edad adecuada. Entre los terrenos con mayor potencial destacan los que se formaron a comienzos del Mioceno, hace entre 23 y 16 millones de años. También quedan zonas por explorar en rocas mucho más antiguas. Para un tramo del Cretácico, hace unos 130 millones de años, los mapas señalan extensas áreas de Rusia y África. Algunos de los restos que interesan a los paleontólogos ya salieron a la luz hace décadas. Se recogieron durante expediciones y hoy forman parte de colecciones de historia natural, donde todavía hay ejemplares pendientes de estudio. Si su lugar de procedencia y su antigüedad coinciden con uno de los vacíos del mapa, revisar ese material podría aportar información sobre qué animales habitaban aquel mar. Para los museos, la herramienta ofrece así un criterio para decidir qué piezas examinar primero.

articles.title: Scientists tracked Manx shearwaters across the Atlantic for two decades and found that fast eastward flights can give birds jet lag; even experienced adults drift off course before correcting their route
articles.summary: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say.
articles.body: Manx shearwaters flying home from feeding trips can be nudged off course by a kind of jet lag, researchers say. It happens when a bird’s body clock falls out of step with the local time. Tracking data from Manx shearwaters on the west coast of the UK revealed that when the birds returned home to their colonies after trips over the Atlantic, their rapid eastward flights disrupted their sense of time and navigation.When humans get jet lag, we fly across time zones and feel tired and out of sync because our body clock is still running on the old time. Shearwaters seem to have a similar problem. For them, it shows up as a wrong turn over the open sea.A studyfinds that long-distance flights can throw seabirds' internal clocks out of sync, causing navigation errors, it was published in October 2026 on the Oxford University website. It talks about how researchers in Oxford University's Department of Biology analysed 20 years of GPS tracking data from 1,045 breeding shearwaters, covering 3,688 foraging trips. The birds set off from colonies on the west coasts of the UK and Ireland. Some flew about 1,000km west to find food. On the way home, they flew east, back to their nests.How a slow body clock sends birds the wrong wayLike many animals, shearwaters use the sun as a compass. This is very useful over open water, where there are no roads or landmarks. But the sun moves across the sky during the day, so a bird needs to know the time to work out where the sun should be. The bird’s body clock gives it that information. It is called the circadian rhythm. Birds normally reset their clocks at sunrise. That works well while a bird stays in one place. But when a bird travels quickly east or west, its clock can fall out of sync with local solar time. On the flight home, the shearwaters crossed places where the sun rises earlier. The Oxford release says this can leave their clocks lagging behind local time by up to around one hour.The researchers worked out how a slow clock should change the birds’ sun compass. Then they compared those predictions with the directions the GPS trackers recorded. As the birds travelled east, they tended to drift clockwise from their expected direction. That is what you would expect if their clocks were running behind. The team from the Department of Biology found that when the predicted compass error pointed towards land, the shearwaters flew closer to the coast. When it pointed away from land, they flew further out to sea. So the birds seem to use the sun compass even when familiar land is close by.Small errors for adults, bigger risks for first-timersThe errors were real, but they were small. In “Seabirds get jet lag, too — and it can throw them a bit off course,” published by Science News on October 29, 2026, Anirban Mukhopadhyay reports that the birds veered by as much as 15 degrees. The errors were small enough to add only a few kilometres to the journey. They were not enough to stop the shearwaters from finding their way home.Adult birds can fix their mistakes because they keep checking where they are. The Oxford team calculated that a shearwater returning from 1,000 km away with an average compass error of seven degrees would fly only about 5 km further than needed to get within 5 km of its colony.“It’s inherently difficult to study the cognitive processes of animals in the wild, so it’s exciting to realise that if we measure their natural movements carefully enough we can reveal the underlying behavioural mechanisms.” - Co-author Professor Tim Guilford, Department of Biology, Oxford University. The consequences could be more significant for animals that cannot continuously reassess and correct their positions. For example, young birds undertaking their first migration could be particularly vulnerable. Small navigational errors might accumulate over a long journey, potentially shifting their eventual destination by hundreds of kilometres.Researchers do not yet know whether the clock mismatch affects the birds in other ways. Internal clocks control many parts of an animal’s behaviour and body, so the problem could reach beyond navigation. More work is needed to find out. Dr Patrick Lewin, the lead researcher, has said that studying animals that regularly travel long distances could one day help us understand how humans cope with jet lag. “It’s amazing to think that billions of migratory animals look up to the sun for direction, relying on clocks silently ticking away inside them, and that errors in those clocks can cause them to take tiny shifts off course.” - Lead researcher Dr Patrick Lewin, Department of Biology, Oxford University.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Rick Wakeman plays Life on Mars? on Mars set in Stevenage
articles.summary: Wakeman says it was a "career first" and his close friend David Bowie would have "loved it".
articles.body:
Veteran keyboard player Rick Wakeman has achieved a "career first" by performing Life on Mars? on a giant sand pit that mimics the surface of the Red Planet.

The performer recreated the part he played on David Bowie's 1973 single release on a digital piano at the Airbus Space Facility in Stevenage, Hertfordshire.

The indoor terrain, about the size of a basketball court, was used to test systems for the ExoMars Rosalind Franklin rover, which Europe plans to send to Mars, with a launch scheduled for 2028.

Wakeman, best known for his solo career and time in the band Yes, said it was the closest he would get to performing on the surface of the Red Planet and that he was sure Bowie would have "loved" the one-off gig.

He first visited the "Mars yard" about seven months ago and "couldn't believe" what he saw.

Wakeman said it was the "most remarkable facility" and that he was impressed with its many features, including the 300 tonnes of specially selected sand, which closely matches the kind found on the planet.

Wakeman used his performance on Friday to launch Return to the Red Planet, his second album release inspired by Mars.

One of the tracks, titled Bowie's Vision, is a tribute to the star, on some of whose albums Wakeman played.

He always wanted to do a "tribute to David" and this latest release provided an opportunity to do that.

"It's not meant to sound like a Bowie track in any way, but it's got a big ending which is David in space really, more than anything else," he said.

Wakeman added that the singer "played a massive part in [his] musical life" and shared his enthusiasm for space.

Wakeman's fascination with space began with Sputnik, the world's first human-made satellite, which was launched in 1957.

He was also fascinated by the story of Yuri Gagarin , the Russian cosmonaut who became the first human to travel into outer space in 1961.

Gagarin completed one orbit of Earth in 108 minutes.

As a child, Wakeman said he did not want to "play cowboys and Indians".

"My mum and dad bought me a little plastic space suit for about three and six from Woolworths or something, and I just wore it all the time," he said.

"And my fascination with space continued. I've got great friends at NASA. A lot of my music NASA has sent up into space, which I argue is the reason the aliens haven't landed here yet because they've taken one listen to my music and gone, 'Oh, we ain't going there.'"

During the gig, Wakeman took questions from fans who had won "golden tickets" to the event.

Brothers Robert and Peter Marsh have been going to concerts together for about 40 years.

The pair said it meant "everything" to be at Wakeman's performance.

The musician said he could not wait until 2030, when the ExoMars rover , named Rosalind Franklin, is scheduled to land on the Red Planet.

When asked whether he believed there had been life on Mars, he said: "I mean, we know it had oceans, it had rivers, and if you've got that, then you must have had life.

"So who knows if there wasn't maybe a life like this two billion years ago? But we find it hard to comprehend. I can't comprehend anything these days."

articles.title: Exclusive: Bedrock Energy raises $24M to build more AI-enabled geothermal drill rigs for enterprise buildings | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Geothermal heat pumps could free up significant space on the grid. Bedrock Energy raised $24 million to bring its AI-guided drill rigs to more markets.
articles.body:
Dig deep enough, and the temperature of the ground remains steady year round, a fun trivia fact that has the potential to improve efficiency and slash costs for heating and cooling across the country.

Geothermal heat pumps, which use the ground as a heat source in winter and heat sink in summer, have been around for decades, but they’re underutilized. Just a fraction of all buildings in the U.S. use them in part because it’s expensive to drill into the earth. But one startup, Bedrock Energy , says its AI-directed rigs can slash drilling times by up to 80%, significantly reducing costs.

That time savings recently helped Bedrock raise a new $24 million funding round, the startup told TechCrunch. Previously, it raised a $12 million Series A in 2025 and an $8.5 million seed round in 2023.

Bedrock has focused mostly on commercial properties to date, since they benefit from deep, accurate boreholes which maximize the use of their small footprints. But the startup has also been talking with data center developers, Joselyn Lai, co-founder and CEO of Bedrock Energy, told TechCrunch. Some might use it for cooling server racks, but others are interested in the technology’s flat load profile — deploying it on neighboring properties can open up significant capacity on the grid.

“We had someone in Michigan say, if we could free up a few megawatts, I think we might be able to operate that many months or even a year earlier,” Lai said. “A year of revenue for a data center is very meaningful.”

Bedrock says its modernized approach to shallow geothermal drilling — up to 1,000 feet or so — sets it apart. Most geothermal heat pump drillers use rigs that are similar to those used for water wells. They work fine, but they’re crude instruments.

Instead, Bedrock uses directional drilling techniques borrowed from the oil and gas industry, guiding them using its own models of the subsurface. That combination allows them to optimize drilling and placement, the company says, helping to ensure performance and longevity. Sensors in the boreholes help to refine those models.

The startup currently operates in Utah, Colorado, New York, Alberta, and its home state of Texas, and the new round will help the company expand into New England, New Jersey, the upper Midwest, and additional states in the West, Lai said.

To power that expansion, Bedrock will add more rigs to its fleet to serve customers in those regions. Currently, it has drilled boreholes in nine sites, and it has secured payments from new customers in anticipation of drilling in the next year or two, she added.

Once up and running, a geothermal heat pump requires far less maintenance than traditional HVAC systems. “You only have to install it once and then it works for a very long time, which is very good for infrastructure from a financial perspective,” Lai said.

The new round was led by Clean Energy Ventures and Clearvision Ventures, with participation from GVP Climate, Susquehanna Sustainable Investments, Catalytic Capital for Climate and Health by Temasek Trust, MUUS, Great Wave Ventures, Autodesk Foundation, Titanium Ventures, Energy Impact Partners, Wireframe Ventures, Elemental Impact, and SFV Capital.

articles.title: Leonids meteor shower to peak this week: How to watch
articles.summary: The Leonids meteor shower is set to put on a show this week, peaking in mid-November each year.
articles.body:
AUSTIN ( KXAN ) — The Leonids meteor shower is set to put on a show this week, peaking in mid-November each year.

The meteor shower gets its name from the radiant constellation Leo. This is where the meteors appear to originate when looking at the sky.

As the comet 5P/Tempel-Tuttle travels near the Sun, small pieces of rock and dust break off, forming the meteors. Those parts then burn up as they enter the Earth’s atmosphere.

5P/Tempel-Tuttle was discovered twice by different people, Ernst Tempel and Horace Tuttle, in 1865 and 1866, respectively, giving it the name.

It is a small comet that takes 33 years to orbit the Sun once.

The Leonids are quite fast — they can travel at speeds of 44 miles per second. They are also bright and can be colorful.

They are best known for fireball meteors, which are characterized by large explosions of light, and Earth-grazers, which have long, colorful tails and track near the horizon.

Although the meteor rates are often as low as three meteors per hour, the Leonids are considered a major meteor shower.

About every 33 years, a Leonid storm occurs with hundreds to thousands of meteors per hour. The difference between a meteor shower and a meteor storm is having at least 1,000 meteors per hour.

A Leonid meteor storm last occurred in 2002. In 1966, a meteor storm led to thousands of meteors entering the atmosphere within 15 minutes, so many that it appeared to “fall like rain,” according to NASA .

The Leonids peak the night of Nov. 16, or Monday night into Tuesday morning.

Viewing is best starting at midnight until dawn. For the best shot at seeing the Leonids, travel outside the city and streetlights to an area with dark skies.

Face your feet towards the east and lie on your back, looking at as large a portion of the sky as possible. It could take up to 30 minutes for your eyes to adapt before you can easily spot meteors.

articles.title: Exclusive: Mazama Energy has a solution for geothermal’s biggest drilling problem | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Khosla-backed Mazama Energy has developed a new way to supercool its geothermal drill bits, letting it drill faster and deeper in a quest to bring down the cost of electricity.
articles.body:
Success in geothermal energy is guided by two basic goals — drill fast and drill deep. Hit both targets, and geothermal startups have a good chance at being cheaper than nearly every other source on the electrical grid.

But while the goals might be straightforward, they’re anything but easy. Drilling fast generates heat, which damages equipment, and so does drilling deep.

Those two foes are what led Mazama Energy to develop a new technology, called Carbon Chill, that uses carbon dioxide to cool the drill bit and bring cuttings to the surface. The technology will not only let the company drill deeper, but also faster. The startup gave TechCrunch an exclusive look at Carbon Chill.

“Our rate of penetration increased 20% over the already very high rates we were achieving,” Sriram Vasantharajan, co-founder and CEO of Mazama Energy, told TechCrunch.

Speed has other advantages in geothermal. Drilling represents about 25% to 30% of the total cost of building a power plant, so reducing drill time can bring costs down significantly.

If geothermal startups succeed in drilling faster and cheaper, they stand to help reshape the grid in the 2030s. Hyperscalers are already planning the facilities that will enter operation at the end of the decade.

Mazama has been working on the problem for years now. In October 2025, the Khosla-backed startup said it had drilled a well in Oregon that reached 629˚ F (331˚ C), and a more recent well has surpassed 700˚ F, Vasantharajan said. In September, the startup raised $135 million in a round led by Centaurus Capital and Doerr Capital.

Mazama hopes that its new carbon dioxide-based cooling technology will help it prove that geothermal energy from super-hot rock is a viable contender in the electricity market.

Already companies like Google and Meta have started to explore the use of geothermal energy, in part because the potential is enormous: A report from the National Laboratory of the Rockies said that geothermal could generate between 26.5 to 57 terawatts of electricity in the U.S. alone. If just 10% of the conservative estimate were developed, it would more than double the U.S.’s peak generating capacity.

Geothermal experts have identified super-hot rock — in which temperatures exceed 752˚ F (400˚ C) — as a promising way to improve the performance of individual wells. At those temperatures, water turns “supercritical,” a gaseous-like liquid state which carries five to 10 times more energy than water from traditional geothermal wells. By harvesting more energy from each well, developers have to drill fewer of them, bringing costs down.

Accessing that heat can be challenging for traditional drilling methods. Most geothermal drillers use “mud” — a combination of water and other compounds to keep the bit cool and clear cuttings from the borehole. But mud can only bring temperatures down so much. Eventually, they become so hot that electronics in the drill bit, which help keep it on course, start to fail.

High temperature-rated electronics exist, but they’d be cost prohibitive, Vasantharajan said.

Instead of mud, Mazama injects liquid carbon dioxide down the center of its drill string. As it travels deeper, it gets heated by the rock around it, which turns it supercritical, too. Then, just before it reaches the drill head, Mazama has it flow through a valve that looks a lot like a rocket nozzle. As the gas expands, it escapes through the cone-shaped nozzle and rapidly cools, absorbing heat from the electronics and the drill bit.

“I look at [carbon dioxide cooling] as a binary,” he said. “Without such technologies, I am, today, not able to drill these horizontal wells at super-hot rock temperatures.”

That capital injection will help Mazama drill more wells deeper. By next year, Vasantharajan said his company hopes to complete a single well that’s capable of generating up to 15 megawatts of electricity.

“What was just a dream or a quest, I can tell you with confidence is now a promise,” he said. “We see a path towards this commercial super-hot rock geothermal.”

articles.summary: Ukraine’s military has been relying on the internet service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.
articles.body:
Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that limits on SpaceX’s Starshield military-grade internet service are disrupting Ukrainian drone operations and hindering the country’s war effort against Russia.

Over the weekend, two people were killed in a Russian jet-powered drone attack on what Ukrainian officials called “critical infrastructure” in the northern Koriukivka region. An energy facility was also hit in Odesa overnight on Sunday, leaving 41,000 households without electricity.

Zelenskyy linked the success of these Russian strikes to limits that he said had been placed on Ukraine’s use of Starshield. The country’s military has been relying on the service since December 2024 to intercept Russian drones.

Starshield is a sister service to Starlink, a network of 11,000 satellites launched into low Earth orbit by SpaceX to provide high-speed internet connectivity, even in remote areas.

In a statement on X on Sunday, Zelenskyy said that Russia was targeting energy substations with Shahed drones, which both sides often use to attack each other.

He added that “many of these strikes are getting through because restrictions on the operating speed of Starshield terminals along the front line and in the temporarily occupied territories are still there”.

“We are counting on these restrictions being lifted. The protection of lives and Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter directly depends on this,” he added.

Zelenskyy also accused Starlink’s sister service of throttling internet speeds and hampering military operations on Saturday. He said that the internet restrictions had been in place for five days.

This is not the first time Ukrainian officials have complained about limits on Starshield hampering Kyiv’s defence efforts.

Last month, Ukrainian defence officials said they had lost access to important satellite-based communications and that the disruptions had affected military missions. This came in the wake of heavy Russian missile and drone strikes, for which Ukraine said it had received no prior warning.

How is slow-speed internet impacting Ukraine’s defences?

According to a November 2 report by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), Starshield is critical to Ukraine since it helps in encrypting satellite communications, which are needed to guide drones in order to carry out interceptions.

“In addition to using Starshield service for strikes within Ukrainian territory occupied by Russian forces, Ukraine uses Starshield-equipped drones to intercept and defend against Russian drones, such as new jet-powered drones taking aim at Ukrainian critical infrastructure and civilian targets,” the CSIS report noted.

Without access to Starshield internet, these Ukrainian drones are unable to work as effectively.

“Our interceptor drones lose connection with their operators at a speed of 161 kilometres per hour (100 miles per hour) and simply cannot catch up with Russian jet-powered ‘shaheds’,” Zelenskyy said on X on Sunday.

After last month’s disruptions, Zelenskyy said on X that “intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues”.

“This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles,” he added.

Last month, Serhiy Beskrestnov, a defence adviser to Zelenskyy, had posted on Telegram that SpaceX had also “implemented a speed limit” on Starlink terminals, capping internet speeds at 100mph (161km/h).

That meant any drones or missiles flying at more than 100mph lost their guidance connection.

“Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions,” he had said, adding that this was clearly “related to the current political situation”.

Officials have said the restrictions have also reduced capabilities for front-line logistics, reconnaissance and relaying signals.

What are the jet-powered drones Russia is using?

Jet-powered drones are high-speed uncrewed aerial vehicles equipped with small turbojet engines rather than traditional propellers or piston engines.

In its war on Ukraine, Russia has increasingly deployed jet-powered variants such as the Geran-3, Geran-4, and Geran-5 models.

These drones fly at much higher speeds than traditional propeller-powered drones, making them significantly harder for Ukrainian air defences to intercept.

In August, 38 people were killed in the village of Myla in Ukraine, when a Russian drone attack struck an ammunition depot. Another 12 were killed in attacks across the country in September.

Ukraine’s Air Force spokesman Yurii Ihnat said in September that while the country has an interception rate of more than 90 percent against propeller-powered drones, that success rate falls to only 60 percent against jet-powered models.

Ukraine has, however, retaliated using its own drone systems, and has also struck Russian refineries, hitting 12 in August, along with two gas-processing plants and three oil shipment terminals, according to its defence ministry.

On Sunday, Ukraine’s army said it also shot down 106 of 132 Russian drones launched overnight.

But to counter Russia’s jet-powered drones more efficiently, Zelenskyy said he had told teams of Ukraine’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Ministry of Defence, and the presidential office “to work as closely as possible with the American side and SpaceX” and remove restrictions on Starshield.

“It is important to be on the right side of history. It is essential to help Ukraine,” he said on Sunday.

Didn’t Trump and Musk say Starshield internet was restored?

Starlink, owned by US billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, is yet to respond to recent accusations about Starshield from Zelenskyy.

But last month, the company and Musk denied restricting internet speeds.

Responding to a post on X by Ukraine’s former Defence Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who said the speed limits were being lifted and demanded unrestricted internet speed, Musk wrote last month, “Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government.”

“Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS,” he said, referring to the US president.

Musk further clarified that Starlink is for “civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company” – an apparent attempt to differentiate it from Starshield.

Zelenskyy said in an interview with the Financial Times last month that US military officials had earlier warned Kyiv that Washington would block intelligence unless attacks on Russian energy infrastructure stop.

The Ukrainian leader added that he did not accept suggestions that the Starshield incident could have been a glitch. “It was not a technical problem; it was the will,” he said.

Tensions between Kyiv and Washington have been building since Donald Trump returned to the presidency last year, including over Washington’s increasing reluctance to militarily support Ukraine and its mounting efforts to forge a deal with Russia.

But Trump has said that it is Musk who controls Starlink’s operations in Ukraine.

When asked about internet restrictions in Ukraine, he told reporters last month that Musk had restored Kyiv’s access, while denying any White House role in the episode.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said last month that decisions about Starlink’s speed and access belong to Musk.

“The bottom line is that that is governed by a private commercial contract as to how ⁠⁠⁠⁠their stuff can be used and what speeds they’ll allow it to be used at,” Rubio had said.

What is the status of Russia-Ukraine negotiations?

Meanwhile, officials from Ukraine and Russia held peace talks in Abu Dhabi, in the United Arab Emirates, last week. The talks, mediated by the US, only yielded an agreement on a prisoner exchange and failed to make a breakthrough on ending the war, which is nearing the five-year mark.

The US, however, pitched a new pathway for Ukraine to join NATO, an aspiration that Kyiv has long held as a means to guarantee its defence against Russia.

According to Zelenskyy, Trump’s administration has suggested that Ukraine would need to agree to give up all of the Donbas region in the country’s east, which Russian President Vladimir Putin has demanded as one of his conditions for ending the war.

On Saturday, Zelenskyy told reporters that the prospect of Ukraine joining NATO in exchange for ceding territory had not been raised by members of the alliance before and reiterated that Kyiv would not give up any of its territories.

But Zelenskyy said if Ukraine received a peace deal which included security guarantees, the right to maintain a strong and well-funded Ukrainian army, and funds to rebuild the country, then he would hold a national referendum on the question of ceding territory in exchange for NATO membership.

The Kremlin has not yet responded to the latest US proposal. But it has maintained a strict position that Ukraine’s NATO membership is a red line for Moscow and a direct threat to Russia’s national security. In fact, Putin has also cited the issue of Ukraine’s NATO aspirations as one reason why Russia launched its war in 2022.

Moscow has, however, insisted that Ukraine should cede sovereignty over the Donbas region, in addition to parts of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson provinces that Russia already occupies.

articles.title: Big Nuclear isn’t worried about the Democrats stopping data centers
articles.summary: They may have a point.﻿
articles.body: Constellation Energy – America’s largest operator of nuclear power plants – does not share Wall Street’s concerns that the Democrats will slow down data center development. On the company’s third-quarter earnings call last week, CEO Joe Dominguez was, for lack of a better word, unbothered as he addressed the blue wave. “I do think we’ve seen a bit of an overreaction in the market to the election results based upon fear that Democrats won’t let data centers get built,” Dominguez said. Many of the Democrats who seized control of the House and Senate in this month’s midterm elections ran on anti-data-center campaigns, which triggered a historic $2.5 trillion sell-off in AI-adjacent stocks that reached well beyond tech to the energy, construction, and materials sectors. Up until a few years ago, many of Constellation’s nuclear power plants were in severe financial distress and in danger of shutting down early. But the data center development boom and its enormous demand for electricity have dramatically reversed the nuclear industry’s fate. Now, Constellation and other companies like it are signing major deals with Big Tech companies to provide power to data centers. Microsoft, for instance, signed a deal with Constellation to fund the revival of a nuclear plant at Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania. (Three Mile Island is the site of what the Nuclear Regulatory Commission refers to as the “most serious accident in US commercial nuclear power plant operating history.”) Constellation also signed major contracts in the third quarter to provide power to Amazon and Google data centers, Dominguez said. Nuclear energy has had bipartisan support for years. The US Department of Energy classifies nuclear as a “clean” energy source because the act of operating a nuclear reactor does not directly produce carbon emissions. This makes nuclear an appealing investment to Big Tech companies that have to balance aggressive data center development with the ambitious climate goals they set long before the AI race took off. Still, nuclear energy has its issues. One of the biggest is nuclear waste, which the US government has not figured out how to dispose of at scale. Big Nuclear and Big Tech also tout these deals as good for the economy and job creation. “The market scare that people got last week was not lost on Democrats,” Dominguez said on the call. “They do not want to be the reason that the economy takes a nosedive by halting data center development.” Of course, Constellation’s future is essentially staked on the data center buildout, and Dominguez’s job is to convince investors they have nothing to worry about. In this instance, however, Dominguez really does seem genuinely unconcerned by the new Democratic majority in the federal government. It could be that he understands that, yes, while the Democrats won the midterms on promises of data center regulation and the blue wave included many new Democratic governors, data centers aren’t necessarily a strictly partisan issue. Some Democrats have opposed harsh measures like moratoriums — though on the flip slide, Constellation may also have to deal with challenges from the other side of the aisle. In Virginia, some of the state lawmakers who have been the most vocal about data centers are actually Republican. Virginia Sen. Richard Stuart, a conservative Republican, has aggressively pursued data center regulation. Last month, Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, denied Stuart’s request for a special session to address a concerning new report from the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality on the state’s groundwater supply, which has become strained amid rampant data center growth. The fight against data centers so far has been highly fragmented and hyperlocal, but that could change soon. The Trump administration loves data centers, and the federal government is working on wresting some control over data center development away from the states. But even then, Democrats and Republicans at the federal level tend to view data centers as an inevitable part of the future that needs some guardrails rather than out-of-control corporate growth infringing on the average American’s quality of life. Just look at the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, which was co-sponsored by two Democrats. The Senate is expected to vote on a passage of a sweeping bill which is being marketed as a way to speed up the permitting process for new power plants and transmission lines and connect new data centers to the grid faster. New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich, one of the Democrats backing the bill, has touted its inclusion of provisions designed to protect utility customers from rising rates due to data centers, ensuring Big Tech pays its fair share of costs. Researchers at Columbia University SIPA’s Center on Global Energy Policy called the bill’s protections “mixed,” noting they do not account for wholesale capacity and energy prices, a “principal way” data center electricity demand can lead to higher household bills. Senate Democrats are sharply divided on the bill, which critics say will fast-track data center projects at the expense of public input and environmental oversight and lead to a massive overbuild of energy projects that Americans will end up paying for. On Constellation’s earnings call, Dominguez pointed out that Virginia and Illinois, states with Democratic governors already in place before the election, have seen “a great deal of data center development.” “The bottom line is that Democrats care deeply about economic growth and they care very deeply about the many labor jobs that go with data center construction,” Dominguez said. “With labor such a key constituent for Democrats, it’s hard to imagine that we are going to halt work …There might be some differences and certainly there are going to be some local areas, I think, that are not going to want data centers.” Of course, Dominguez is speaking to investors here, and he wants to assuage their concerns. He also has a good point. Grassroots efforts to stop local data center development have been successful and have contributed to broader opposition to data center development across the country. But data center developers can also abandon projects and go elsewhere. Until a few years ago, data centers were largely concentrated in Northern Virginia, but with the AI boom, developers have fanned out across the country in search of available power and land. A total of 38 states have welcomed them with open arms and generous tax breaks, per the National Conference of State Legislatures. Thanks to the convoluted way the US electric grid and energy markets work, Constellation’s power plants don’t even need to be located in the same state as their data center customers — the plant supplying the power just needs to be connected to the same region from which the grid is drawing power. The purchase agreement, in that sense, is symbolic: Because the data center needs more electricity than it can draw from the local grid without causing disruptions for everyone else, the data center pays for independent power providers like Constellation to supply the grid with extra electricity. That’s why data centers and the enormous amount of electricity Big Tech says it needs to power them have been such a boon for the nuclear industry. For years, companies like Constellation have been sitting on a bunch of old reactors teetering on the edge of extinction because they didn’t have enough customers to keep them afloat. Nuclear lobbyists will tell you that’s because the NRC’s safety regulations are overly restrictive and lead to untenable upfront capital costs that make projects impossible to finance. (This has been an industry talking point since 1979, after the NRC seriously overhauled its safety standards following the partial meltdown at Three Mile Island. That site is now owned by Constellation, which has signed a 20-year deal with Microsoft.) Both the Biden and Trump administrations have worked to support the development of nuclear power in the US by passing developer tax credits. The Trump administration has gone even further, pushing for a sweeping reform of the NRC that would make it much easier for new reactors to obtain operating licenses. And the Department of Energy this month approved a $5 billion loan to Constellation, which the company will use to upgrade its existing nuclear fleet. Another nuclear energy company, Vistra, received a $4.2 billion loan. It’s not totally unlike the Biden administration’s passage of the Civil Nuclear Credit Program in 2022, which planned to loan $6 billion to struggling nuclear companies in the US. That’s not lost on Dominguez. “Interestingly, in many respects the election had the Republicans saying a lot of the same things that the Democrats were saying,” Dominguez told investors on the call. “And I believe that the policy solutions are going to be somewhat similar.”

articles.title: Scientists tracked 3,285 harvester ant colonies for 34 years and found the opposite of ordinary aging: older colonies were less likely to die and more likely to reproduce, with some surviving over 40 years
articles.summary: Aging is usually defined by a loss of strength, a loss of fertility and an increase in the probability of death.
articles.body: Aging is usually defined by a loss of strength, a loss of fertility and an increase in the probability of death. But for western harvester ants, growing older offers a surprising benefit. Their colonies do not grow weaker with time, but stronger and better at reproducing. These insect communities defy conventional thinking about aging, and some colonies have lived for more than 40 years, a remarkable scientific investigation spanning 34 years shows.Three decades of research show strange patternThe UH said the research was done by University of Houston biologists Blaine Cole and Diane Wiernasz, Department of Biology and Biochemistry, who studied thousands of western harvester ant colonies in Mesa County, Colo. The scientists started monitoring the colonies in 1992 and analyzed 34 years of observations of 3,285 colonies of known age. The research published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences found a phenomenon they called negative senescence.Phys Org explains that this biological pattern occurs when survival rates and reproductive success increase, not decrease, with age. Older colonies reproduction and survival were higher than younger colonies. In 2024, researchers found 51 colonies between 40 and 42 years old that were established before monitoring began.How ant colonies avoid the effects of agingAs per the report, this is due to the very organized structure of an ant colony, which scientists call a superorganism. It has been reported by the University website that ants form specialized societies with different functions. Worker ants forage, clean the nest, and care for the young after the queen lays the eggs. The main difference is that worker ants usually live about one year while a queen can live for decades. This constant replacement of workers allows the colony to maintain a functioning workforce even as the community as a whole ages, according to the University of Houston.This arrangement, the researchers say, is called a replaceable soma. Biologically, the soma is the part of an organism that does not reproduce. With older workers dying off and younger ones replacing them the working population of the colony is comparatively new for the life of the colony. Importantly, the discovery does not mean that individual ants escape biological aging. Instead, it is a phenomenon at the level of the whole colony.Bigger colonies have more survival advantagesThe size of the colony also turned out to be an important factor in the research. They found that larger colonies had lower mortality rates and greater reproductive success. Interestingly, they were not growing at the expense of reproduction, defying the assumption that organisms must compromise on reproductive output to sustain themselves.The findings give a new lens on the biological mechanisms of longevity, especially in species with very organized social structures, Phys Org noted.What the discovery means for research on agingNegative senescence has been observed in some plants, fish and sea urchins before. But the harvester ant study is good evidence that social organization and the constant replacement of workers can help biological systems to be unusually long-lasting. Now researchers want to know if other highly social insects, like leaf-cutter ants and termites, show similar patterns.The findings also show the importance of long-term scientific observation, according to the University of Houston. Tracking thousands of colonies for decades, researchers discovered a biological pattern that might have been missed by shorter studies.Ultimately, the research is an interesting reminder that aging does not follow a universal biological timetable. In the highly-organised world of the harvester ant, the older you get the more likely you are to survive.Image Courtesy: University of HoustonYour child uses AI every day. But do they understand it? articles.title: Scientists spent 10 days searching Fiji's seas for a bird believed to number fewer than 50 worldwide but saw none; instead, they uncovered the only known recording of its call, deepening the mystery of its survival.
articles.summary: Somewhere deep in the forests of Fiji, there's a bird holding on to its survival.
articles.body: Somewhere deep in the forests of Fiji, there's a bird holding on to its survival. Ten days of research and hours of searching to locate one of the rarest seabirds in the world, believed to number fewer than 50 individuals, still left researchers without answers. Where it lives, where it breeds or exactly how many are left in the wild remains a mystery to researchers.The story is about the Fiji petrel, believed to inhabit the forests and waters surrounding Fiji's Gau Island. Scientists have been unable to detect even a single bird, but what they found was beyond expectations: a recording of the bird's call, which might help them understand a species whose very survival remains shrouded in mystery.According to a study published in Bird Conservation International, researchers from National Geographic Pristine Seas, BirdLife International and NatureFiji-MareqetiViti conducted a targeted expedition around Fiji's Gau Island in May 2025. Despite more than 45 hours of searching using bait, spotlights and acoustic attraction techniques, the team failed to record a confirmed sighting of the critically endangered Fiji petrel.Lindsay Young, Vice President of Research for Pristine Seas and expedition leader, said in the official BirdLife International announcement of November 12, 2026: “We’re in a race against time to save the Fiji Petrel.” She further explained: “We searched for the bird night and day through the most tried-and-true techniques available, but the Fiji Petrel eluded us. While we left Gau still chasing shadows, communities’ commitment to habitat protection and invasive species control gives any remaining Fiji Petrels a fighting chance.”A bird that has remained a mystery for decadesThe story of the Fiji petrel goes back to 1855, when British naturalist John MacGillivray first collected a specimen of the bird on Gau Island. For nearly 130 years, there were no further confirmed sightings, leaving ornithologists uncertain about whether the species still existed. Some even feared it had become extinct. It was not until 1984 that an adult Fiji petrel was spotted again, when it flew into the spotlight of researcher Dick Watling during an expedition on the island. The bird was examined, photographed and subsequently released.Even after its rediscovery, the species remained exceptionally difficult to study. Researchers have recorded only 22 confirmed sightings at sea and 16 grounded birds found on land, all associated with Gau Island. Despite decades of research and several expeditions, scientists have never managed to locate a single nesting site. This has made it difficult to understand its breeding habits, population size and feeding behaviour.The mystery is also deeply connected to the island's local history. Known to residents as Kacau ni Gau, the bird has a place in traditional songs and oral histories passed down through generations. Yet, as modern sightings have become increasingly scarce, even the communities that have lived alongside the species have limited opportunities to observe it. The last confirmed sighting on land dates back to 2012, while the most recent confirmed sighting at sea was recorded during a scientific expedition in 2023.For researchers, finding the bird's nesting grounds is now particularly important. The species is believed to breed in the mountainous forests of Gau Island, but its exact habitat remains unknown. Without locating these sites, conservationists face considerable challenges in protecting the areas where the remaining birds may be reproducing.What did the latest expedition uncover?aThe expedition may not have found the bird researchers were hoping to see, but it did bring them closer to understanding the mystery surrounding its survival. During their May 2025 expedition around Gau Island, the team used several methods to attract and locate the Fiji petrel, including chumming, spotlighting and acoustic attraction techniques. However, despite spending more than 45 hours searching, they failed to record a single confirmed sighting.One of the most interesting findings emerged through conversations with the local community. Researchers learnt about an existing recording of a Fiji petrel's call, captured from a fledgling that had been found grounded near Nukuloa Primary School on Gau Island. The recording offered a rare acoustic reference for scientists trying to identify the species in the wild. It is particularly valuable because very little is known about the bird's vocalisations and behaviour.The expedition also brought attention to the importance of involving local communities in conservation. Researchers met village chiefs and residents to discuss protecting the island's forests, particularly the mountainous areas believed to contain the bird's nesting grounds. Community members expressed their commitment to strengthening efforts to control invasive species, which pose a threat to native wildlife and their habitats.Although the team returned without locating a single Fiji petrel, the expedition was not entirely without progress. The existing recording, local knowledge and renewed conservation commitments have given researchers additional clues to work with. For a species whose nesting grounds remain undiscovered and whose population is believed to number fewer than 50, even these small discoveries could prove important.Your child uses AI every day. articles.title: Scientists played recordings of unborn crocodiles calling from inside their eggs and found that mothers began digging only when the sounds became continuous, revealing how hatchlings signal when they are ready to emerge
articles.summary: A crocodile nest can remain undisturbed for hours even after the young inside the eggs begin making sounds.
articles.body: A crocodile nest can remain undisturbed for hours even after the young inside the eggs begin making sounds. The mother may hear them, turn towards the nest or shift her position, yet still leave the eggs covered. Scientists investigating this behaviour in Nile crocodiles have found that the timing of these calls matters. According to the study published in Animal Behaviour, titled, Crocodile mothers’ response to hatching calls’, their experiments involved playing recordings of unborn crocodiles vocalising from inside their eggs and observing how the mothers responded. The females did not begin digging simply because they heard a call. They waited until the sounds became continuous, suggesting that the adults use a particular pattern of communication to decide when their offspring are ready to emerge.How hatching calls help crocodile embryos communicate before birthFor Nile crocodiles (Crocodylus niloticus), communication between offspring and parents begins before the young have broken through their shells. Embryos nearing the end of their development produce distinctive vocal sounds while still inside their eggs. These are known as hatching calls, and they serve more than one purpose.The sounds can be heard by other embryos in the nest as well as by the female guarding it. Within the clutch, calls help coordinate the timing of hatching, allowing young crocodiles to emerge around the same period rather than at widely separated intervals. The mother also responds to these sounds, eventually helping the hatchlings by uncovering the nest.What makes mother crocodiles respond to calls from their unborn youngThere is often a gap between the first sounds produced by embryos and the moment the female begins opening the nest. That delay raised a question for scientists: if the mother can hear the calls, what determines when she decides to act?To investigate, researchers used recordings of hatching calls and played them to female Nile crocodiles. By controlling the sounds presented to the animals, they could examine whether particular patterns of vocalisation prompted different responses.The females were capable of detecting even individual calls. When they heard isolated sounds, they sometimes turned their heads or moved their bodies towards the source. These reactions indicated that the vocalisations had caught their attention. But listening and digging were two different responses.An occasional call was not enough to make a female uncover the nest. The behaviour changed when the recordings consisted of sustained sequences of calls, continuing for several tens of seconds. It was this prolonged pattern that prompted the females to begin digging.Continuous calling appears to signal that the hatchlings are readyThe difference between a scattered series of sounds and a sustained burst may help explain why crocodile mothers do not respond to every call they hear. Embryos within a nest do not all begin vocalising at the same time. Some may start calling while others are still developing, meaning that the sounds can initially be intermittent. Waiting for calls to become continuous may give the female a more reliable indication that several embryos are reaching the hatching stage. The sustained noise could therefore act as a signal that enough of the clutch is ready for the mother to intervene.The response also has implications for synchronised hatching. When several embryos vocalise in succession, the mother receives a stronger indication that hatching is under way across the nest. Her decision to dig at that point may help the young emerge within a closer time frame.Role of communication in crocodile parenting before birthThe findings suggest that crocodile mothers do not simply become more likely to dig every time they hear another call. Instead, their response appears to depend on whether the vocal activity reaches a particular threshold.A mother may register individual sounds and react to them without taking any action that disturbs the nest. Digging begins only after the calls continue for long enough, indicating that the pattern and duration of the signals matter alongside their presence.For Nile crocodiles, the sounds coming from beneath the ground are not necessarily an immediate instruction to dig. The mother appears to wait for a more sustained chorus before deciding that it is time to uncover the eggs.Your child uses AI every day. But do they understand it?
